documents.abstract: Background Artificial intelligence (AI) is spreading through health care, yet systems that administer assessments directly to clients remain untested in occupational therapy (OT), where the initial assessment both gathers data and builds therapeutic rapport. Objective To compare user experience of a purpose-built, remote AI-administered OT initial assessment with a human-administered assessment. Methods Thirty adults completed an AI-administered and a human-administered OT initial assessment in randomized order one to two weeks apart (crossover design), rating usability, perceived compassion, goal setting and satisfaction after each and stating an overall preference; 28 gave reflection interviews. Formats were compared within participants (Wilcoxon signed-rank, McNemar, Holm-corrected) and interviews analyzed thematically. Results Participants were randomized 15 per sequence; order affected no outcome. AI usability was high (modified System Usability Scale 81.1). Perceived compassion favored the human format (median 9.90 vs 7.53; Hodges–Lehmann difference 2.39, 95% CI 1.56–3.11; p < 0.001), as did satisfaction (all p < 0.001). Agreement that goals were clear, personalized, relevant, attainable and motivating did not differ (all p ≥ 0.25), but strong agreement was more frequent after the human format on four of five items (40.0–53.3 percentage points, all p ≤ 0.002). Overall, 83% (25/30) preferred the human format. Four themes were identified. Conclusions The AI-administered assessment was highly usable and produced goals accepted as clear, relevant and attainable at rates matching the human format; what differed was the depth of endorsement, perceived compassion and preference. Conversational AI appears better placed to supplement therapist-led assessment than to replace it.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has become a new participant in everyday and educational communication. Learners now talk to chatbots, use machine translation and receive automated feedback on their writing. This conceptual paper examines how these tools affect the development of sociolinguistic thinking, understood as the ability to select, interpret and adapt language forms according to social context, participants and communicative goals. Drawing on sociocultural theory, social learning theory, sociolinguistics and intercultural pedagogy, the paper outlines the cognitive, social and emotional mechanisms involved and analyzes the opportunities and risks of AI as a language model and interlocutor. It then proposes five pedagogical conditions for developing sociolinguistic thinking in AI-supported learning environments: critical AI literacy, contextualized task design, teacher mediation, comparison of human and machine language, and a supportive psychological climate.

This study describes the development and realization of an intelligent plastic waste sorting system that combines computer vision, robotic control, and a graphical user interface (GUI) for real-time monitoring. The system integrates the You Only Look Once version 8 (YOLOv8) deep learning architecture to detect and classify seven distinct plastic types: polyethylene terephthalate (PET), high-density polyethylene (HDPE), single-use plastics, single-layer plastics, multi-layer plastics, squeeze tubes, and ultra-high-temperature (UHT) boxes. Sorting actions are executed by an EEZYbotARM Mk2 robotic arm, driven by an STM32F446RE microcontroller, which performs autonomous pick-and-place operations according to the recognition output. A custom interface built with Python Qt version 5 (PyQt5) enables live video visualization, delineation of detection areas, counting of identified categories, and additional functionalities such as counter reset, selective filtering, and exporting detection records to Excel. The complete setup was tested on a conveyor-based system, confirming high detection precision, dependable robotic operation, and a user-friendly supervision interface. The trained YOLOv8 model achieves a precision of 94%, recall of 95%, and mean average precision (mAP) at Intersection over Union (IoU) thresholds 0.5–0.95 of 94% across the seven plastic waste categories, confirming the effectiveness of the proposed detection pipeline. This contribution aims to mitigate the limited advancement of plastic recycling technologies in developing regions, offering a cost-effective and practical framework for enhancing plastic waste management.

STEM education is a national priority in Malaysia; however, clear gaps in learning outcomes and student participation remain, particularly in rural areas. In Sabah, very low Indeks STEM Murid (ISM) scores, coupled with declining enrolment in the STEM Package A stream, indicate persistent challenges in the quality and continuity of STEM learning at the lower secondary level. These trends suggest that many students do not experience STEM learning as sufficiently meaningful or structured to build confidence and sustain their interest in STEM pathways. This paper reports Phase 1A of a Design and Development Research (DDR) study, focusing on the needs analysis and conceptualisation of EDP.AI, an AI-assisted module designed to scaffold the Engineering Design Process (EDP) for lower secondary students in rural Sabah. Document analysis was conducted to examine challenges related to STEM learning, EDP implementation, artificial intelligence in education, and Cognitive Load Theory (CLT) in low-resource contexts. The evidence was synthesised using design rationale mapping to translate theoretical and contextual insights into actionable design decisions. The outcomes of Phase 1A include the identification of key needs and challenges, the formulation of preliminary design requirements and design principles, and the development of a conceptual model to guide the design of EDP.AI. The proposed module emphasises step-by-step scaffolding aligned with EDP stages, reduced cognitive load, low-bandwidth accessibility, and support for both student reasoning and teacher workload. Overall, this study provides a theoretical and contextual foundation for the subsequent development and expert validation of EDP.AI to support more meaningful and sustainable STEM learning experiences in rural schools.

documents.abstract: As gig workers receive inadequate support from digital labor platforms and (inter)national institutions, many face systemic challenges—such as income insecurity, algorithmic management, and social isolation—and turn to online communities instead. Identification with such shared spaces is fundamental to fostering relational connections and collective practices that help workers cope and succeed. However, these spaces remain poorly understood. This study examines how social media affordances and gig work type shape what social identity scholars call a “common voice” (i.e., the collective expression of identification in an online community). Using computational sentiment analysis and quantitative content analysis of 8,319 posts and 153,440 comments from six of the largest Reddit communities for gig workers, the study finds that common voices emerge, despite the atomizing characteristics of gig work (e.g., geographic dispersion and platform mediation) and the constraint of social cues on the platform that hosts the community. Moreover, common voices significantly differ between platform-specific communities and generic communities for gig workers in themes, sentiments, message length and image use. These findings extend scholarship on gig work, identification, and social media affordances by highlighting their intersection—showing how gig worker communities can act as digital collectives that foster identification and work relationships.

The rapid advancement of digital technologies, including the internet, social media, e-commerce platforms, online marketplaces, and artificial intelligence-based applications, has fundamentally transformed consumer behavior in the digital marketplace. Consumers are no longer passive recipients of marketing messages; instead, they actively seek information, evaluate alternatives, engage with brands, and make purchasing decisions through various digital channels. This transformation has led to the emergence of Digital Consumer Behavior as a critical determinant of marketing effectiveness and business sustainability in the digital economy. This study aims to examine the influence of Digital Consumer Behavior on Consumer Trust and Purchase Decision, as well as to investigate the mediating role of Consumer Trust in this relationship. A quantitative research approach was employed using a survey method involving 100 active digital platform users who had conducted online purchases within the previous six months. Respondents were selected through purposive sampling, and data were analyzed using Structural Equation Modeling–Partial Least Squares (SEM-PLS). The empirical findings reveal that Digital Consumer Behavior has a positive and significant effect on Consumer Trust and Purchase Decision. Furthermore, Consumer Trust significantly influences Purchase Decision. The mediation analysis demonstrates that Consumer Trust significantly mediates the relationship between Digital Consumer Behavior and Purchase Decision. The coefficient of determination indicates that the model explains of the variance in Consumer Trust of the variance in Purchase Decision having a strong relationship. These findings provide theoretical support for the integration of digital consumer behavior and consumer trust perspectives within contemporary marketing literature. From a managerial perspective, businesses should focus on delivering informative, interactive, and trustworthy digital experiences to strengthen consumer trust and enhance purchasing decisions. The study concludes that technological advancements have significantly reshaped how consumers acquire information, build trust, evaluate product alternatives, and make purchasing decisions in a faster, more efficient, and increasingly rational manner.

Digital pathology, driven by whole-slide imaging (WSI), digital slide management, and computational image analysis, is increasingly transforming veterinary diagnostic pathology. The integration of artificial intelligence (AI), including machine learning and deep learning, provides opportunities to automate or assist tasks such as lesion detection, tissue segmentation, mitotic figure identification, immunohistochemistry quantification, and morphometric analysis. However, successful implementation requires more than scanner acquisition or algorithm development. This chapter presents a practice-oriented overview of digital pathology and AI in veterinary diagnostic pathology, emphasizing the complete workflow from tissue processing and slide preparation to scanning, digital viewing, reporting, validation, and quality management. Major pre-analytic, analytic, and post-analytic sources of error are discussed, together with principles for validating whole-slide imaging for primary diagnosis and maintaining ongoing quality assurance. The chapter also describes major AI task types, annotation and ground-truth challenges, performance evaluation, external validation, model monitoring, and responsible deployment. Particular attention is given to veterinary-specific challenges, including species and breed heterogeneity, stain variability, domain shift, limited annotated datasets, data governance, and automation bias. Emerging approaches such as foundation models, self-supervised learning, multimodal integration, and federated learning are also considered. Overall, effective digital pathology adoption depends on rigorous validation, continuous quality management, appropriate interpretation, and pathologist-led diagnostic accountability. Keywords Keywords: Digital pathology; whole-slide imaging; artificial intelligence; computational pathology; veterinary diagnostic pathology; machine learning;

documents.abstract: Rapid urbanization has intensified congestion, pollution, and inefficiencies in transportation systems, necessitating sustainable and intelligent mobility solutions. Smart mobility has emerged as a transformative approach driven by digital transformation and advanced technologies. This chapter examines the role of the Internet of Things (IoT), Artificial Intelligence (AI), Machine Learning (ML), Big Data Analytics, and Cloud Computing in enhancing operational efficiency, real-time decision-making, and service integration. It conceptualizes smart mobility through Mobility-as-a-Service (MaaS), enabling seamless coordination among stakeholders. Drawing on global and Indian examples, the chapter highlights the impact of digital platforms and electric mobility. It also addresses challenges such as infrastructure limitations, regulatory complexity, data privacy, and the digital divide. Finally, it proposes a framework for sustainable, efficient, and user-centric smart mobility systems.

Saudi Arabia’s insurance sector is expanding while simultaneously undergoing regulatory, technological and organizational transformation. Under Vision 2030, digital infrastructure, data and artificial intelligence have become explicit enablers of insurance-sector development, creating a strong policy context for redesigning underwriting. This paper examines how digital transformation can improve risk selection, pricing adequacy and operational efficiency in Saudi insurance underwriting while preserving governance, fairness and professional accountability. An integrative review approach is used to synthesize recent peer-reviewed insurance, artificial-intelligence and financial-technology literature with official Saudi policy and market evidence. The analysis identifies five mutually dependent transformation capabilities: integrated and high-quality data, advanced analytics and artificial intelligence, digitally orchestrated workflows, model governance and explainability, and underwriting talent capable of combining actuarial judgment with digital tools. The paper argues that the greatest value does not arise from replacing underwriters, but from redesigning underwriting as a human-in-the-loop decision system in which routine cases can be automated, complex risks are escalated, and pricing decisions are supported by transparent analytics. Saudi market evidence demonstrates rapid premium growth and an increasingly explicit regulatory focus on technology, data and artificial intelligence. However, implementation risks include fragmented data, algorithmic bias, privacy and cybersecurity concerns, legacy-system integration, model drift and inadequate change management. A Saudi Underwriting Digital Transformation Framework is therefore proposed, linking digital foundations, analytics, workflow redesign, governance safeguards and measurable performance outcomes. The framework provides a research and managerial agenda for insurers seeking to improve technical profitability, customer responsiveness and market resilience while aligning digital underwriting with the objectives of Vision 2030.

Within the framework of the European Erasmus+ STIAEM project, the authors of this study deconstruct the assumed homogeneity of “digital natives” regarding generative artificial intelligence adoption. Utilizing a sample of 2,052 secondary school students, the research architecture applies confirmatory factor analysis, extended Bayesian information criterion graphical least absolute shrinkage and selection operator network analysis, and latent profile analysis. Results identify distinct student profiles based on engagement and familiarity, revealing a profound relational decoupling between technological motivation and situated ethical choices. Under academic deadline pressures, nearly all (92.74%) of the sample participants succumbed to automation bias, uncritically accepting machine hallucinations. This behavioral paradox demonstrates that superficial digital fluency masks severe deficits in epistemic validation and independent thought. Consequently, in this paper the authors argue for shifting from product to process evaluation and integrating explicit algor-ethics interventions within school curricula to develop reflexive, human-centric algorithmic citizenship.

Existing research shows that generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) increases instructional design efficiency. However, there are concerns about pedagogical quality, accuracy and content bias. While prior studies address student passivity in evaluating AI content, the potential for designers to be passive in creating instructional materials remains largely unexplored. This article addresses design safeguards for AI-assisted course and learning-material development through two complementary tools: the Discernment Map, an evaluation checkpoint for instructional designers, and a set of design heuristics. The study is conceptual and design-oriented: both tools were drafted from the literature on AI fluency, automation bias and schema theory, and then refined through structured consultations with six experienced instructional designers in higher education. Though yet to be empirically validated, the practice-informed tools work at two levels: the Map operationalises human oversight of AI outputs across Product, Process and Performance dimensions for each AI-generated artefact, while the heuristics extend discernment into the design of the learning experience itself, so that learners must evaluate rather than accept AI outputs. Both are agile micro-governance tools that integrate critical judgment directly into design workflows. The approach is intended to protect long-term instructional quality against the collective erosion that unchecked AI adoption risks, and to support intentional engagement with AI that reduces automation bias.

documents.abstract: Background Collaborative Reasoning (CR) is a dialogic, learner-centered instructional approach shown to promote learners’ higher-order thinking. However, existing research has paid less attention to how learners engage in CR processes and how the temporal dynamics of engagement relate to the development of individual reasoning. Aims To address this gap, this study investigated the temporal development of behavioral, emotional, and cognitive engagement during CR discussions and examined how evolving engagement patterns were associated with subsequent individual reasoning. Sample The participants were 29 seventh-graders from a middle school in China. The students formed four discussion groups, and each group participated in seven CR discussions. Methods The 28 discussions were video-coded for cognitive, emotional, and behavioral interactions (6868 codes). Process mining and epistemic network analysis were used to model shifts in engagement patterns. Individual reasoning was assessed through post-discussion essays. Results Engagement patterns shifted dynamically over time, moving from socially shared regulation to sustained knowledge co-construction. Groups differed in the timing and trajectory of this transition: some groups shifted earlier, whereas others engaged in prolonged regulatory exchanges. The group characterized by later transitions produced fewer basic argumentative elements but more advanced elements in their individual essays. Conclusions This study highlights dynamic engagement patterns as an important link between collaborative processes and learning outcomes and underscores the importance of understanding temporal configurations of regulation and knowledge co-construction in collaborative learning.

The continuous advancement of remote sensing technology has enabled high-resolution Earth observation; however, interpreting these expansive images using modern Vision Foundation Models (VFMs) remains a significant challenge. Unlike object-centric natural images, remote sensing imagery is fundamentally characterized by extreme target sparsity and massive spatial redundancy. Key objects of interest (e.g., ships, vehicles, scattered buildings) often occupy less than 1% of the spatial extent, surrounded by vast, target-free backgrounds. Many existing VFMs rely on uniform dense processing (e.g., Vision Transformers), while a substantial branch adopts pixel-reconstruction pre-training paradigms (e.g., Masked Autoencoders). These designs may waste substantial computational capacity on modeling redundant backgrounds and dilute the feature representations of small, sparse targets. To bridge this structural misalignment, we propose DynamicVis , a remote sensing visual foundation model explicitly tailored to spatial sparsity in high-resolution imagery, with a focus on large-scale visual pre-training and transferable spatial representations for diverse downstream perception tasks. Architecturally, DynamicVis introduces a Dynamic Region-Aware State Space Model (SSM) that bypasses uniform computation. It adaptively routes and incrementally models only task-relevant, high-salience tokens while employing a parameter-free integration for background context, drastically reducing the complexity of processing ultra-long 2D token sequences ( ∼ 100,000). Crucially, to equip the network with robust spatial-selection capabilities, we propose a novel weakly supervised Region-Level Meta-Embedding Multi-Instance Learning (MIL) pre-training paradigm. Trained on a million-scale dataset, this paradigm promotes foreground-aware regional discrimination in the latent semantic space, mitigating the semantic ambiguity of conventional pixel-reconstruction methods. Extensive evaluations across nine diverse downstream visual perception tasks reveal that DynamicVis achieves competitive performance across region-, instance-, and pixel-level remote sensing tasks, with particularly strong results in sparse-target and instance-level perception tasks (e.g., small object detection and instance segmentation). Notably, DynamicVis processes high-resolution imagery (2048 × 2048) with merely 97 ms latency and 833 MB of memory consumption without employing any acceleration techniques (approximately 6% and 3% of a base ViT, respectively), offering a favorable trade-off between computational scalability and representation accuracy for multi-granular remote sensing analysis. Source code is available at https://github.com/KyanChen/DynamicVis .

The emergence of artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming contemporary education and challenging established assumptions underlying educational theories. This study aims to examine the challenges posed by AI in the intelligence era and analyze the need for reorientation of contemporary educational theories in response to increasingly complex human–AI interactions. A qualitative systematic literature review was conducted using scholarly literature from Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar, with emphasis on publications from 2019 to 2026. The literature was analyzed through thematic analysis and critical interpretive synthesis, guided by the PRISMA 2020 framework, focusing on knowledge construction, learning processes, assessment, teacher and learner agency, ethics, and educational purposes. The findings indicate that AI is reshaping education through personalized learning, adaptive instruction, automated feedback, and expanded knowledge exploration, while simultaneously creating challenges related to knowledge reliability, learner dependency, academic integrity, assessment validity, data privacy, and human agency. The review further shows that constructivism, experiential learning, social learning, connectivism, and humanistic education remain relevant but require critical reorientation to accommodate AI-mediated learning environments. The study proposes a human-centered, AI-augmented educational paradigm that integrates technological intelligence with critical thinking, learner autonomy, teacher agency, ethical reasoning, reflective judgment, and meaningful human interaction.

documents.abstract: Recommender systems (RSs) increasingly support self-regulated learning (SRL) through personalized resources, feedback, and strategy recommendations. However, traditional content based and collaborative filtering approaches suffer from cold start problems, while machine or deep learning methods raise interpretability concerns and LLM-based recommenders require evaluation of explanation faithfulness and hallucinations. This systematic review examines SRL-oriented recommender algorithms from an algorithmic and pedagogical perspective. Six databases were searched using predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria, yielding 25 eligible studies published between 2020 and 2025. The review traces the evolution from traditional filtering methods to machine or deep learning and emerging LLM-based approaches. Three major challenges were identified: cold start, limited explainability, and LLM hallucinations, alongside gaps in learner system interaction and metacognitive scaffolding. Future SRL-RS research should compare algorithms under controlled data sparsity, evaluate explanation faithfulness and source curation, preserve learner agency, integrate SRL strategies across three phases, and longitudinally assess SRL skill maintenance and transfer.

documents.abstract: With the widespread use of the Internet and digital technologies, online health information-seeking behavior has become an important factor associated with the patient–physician relationship. This review aimed to evaluate the relationship between online health information-seeking behavior and the patient–physician relationship in light of the current literature. English-language articles published between 2016 and 2026 were identified through a search of the PubMed database, and studies related to online health information-seeking behavior, the patient–physician relationship, health literacy, trust in physicians, and artificial intelligence were examined using a narrative review approach. The findings indicate that the relationship between online health information-seeking behavior and the patient–physician relationship is associated with the reliability of health information, health and eHealth literacy, trust in physicians, patient-centered communication, and individual characteristics. Reliable online health information has been associated with higher levels of patient engagement and shared decision-making, whereas inaccurate or misleading information has been associated with higher levels of health anxiety and problems related to trust and communication. Although artificial intelligence–supported applications may contribute to patient education, physician oversight is required for their safe use. Encouraging reliable sources of health information and supporting digital health literacy by healthcare professionals may contribute to strengthening a trust-based patient–physician relationship.

With the rapid proliferation of electric vehicles, the safety and reliability of lithium-ion batteries have become critical concerns. Effective anomaly detection is essential for ensuring safe battery operation. However, as battery systems and operating scenarios become increasingly complex, Battery fault diagnosis and maintenance increasingly require stronger adaptability to heterogeneous operating scenarios and intelligent human–AI collaboration. Traditional fault detection and diagnosis paradigms are usually tailored to specific scenarios and predefined workflows, making them less effective in complex real-world applications. To address the scarcity of open-source battery fault report corpora and the lack of unified maintenance knowledge representation, this study investigates a descriptive text modeling approach for battery signal reports. Monitoring signals, statistical features, anomaly records, and state assessment results are transformed into structured and readable natural language descriptions, thereby constructing a language corpus for battery health diagnosis and maintenance. Based on this framework, we propose VBFDD-Agent, a vehicle battery fault detection and diagnosis agent for automotive-grade battery systems. VBFDD-Agent integrates descriptive battery-state texts, historical case retrieval, local maintenance manuals, and large language model reasoning to generate structured diagnostic results and maintenance recommendations. Experimental results show that the proposed framework can accurately perform anomaly monitoring and provide flexible, efficient, and actionable maintenance suggestions. Expert evaluation further confirms the practical value of the generated recommendations.

Nephrology nursing has evolved significantly over the past decades, transitioning from task-oriented care to a comprehensive, patient-centered specialty that integrates clinical expertise, advanced technology, and chronic disease management.This review explores the emerging roles of nephrology nurses in the current healthcare landscape and envisions future directions shaped by technological advancements, healthcare reforms, and evolving patient needs.Current roles encompass not only hemodialysis and peritoneal dialysis care but also kidney transplantation, conservative kidney management, patient education, and multidisciplinary collaboration.The increasing prevalence of chronic kidney disease and the complexity of renal replacement therapies demand advanced competencies, including leadership, research, and quality improvement.Future roles are anticipated to expand into telehealth, remote patient monitoring, artificial intelligence-assisted care, genomics-informed nursing, and community-based kidney health promotion.The integration of advanced practice nursing and nurseled clinics is expected to further strengthen chronic disease management and reduce hospital readmissions.This review highlights the need for continuous professional development, specialized training programs, and policy support to equip nephrology nurses for these evolving responsibilities.Emerging nephrology nursing roles are critical to addressing the global burden of kidney disease and enhancing the quality, accessibility, and sustainability of kidney care delivery.

High-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) is one of the most widely employed analytical techniques for the qualitative and quantitative determination of compounds. Despite its exceptional sensitivity and reliability, conventional HPLC method development and data interpretation often require extensive experimental optimization, expert knowledge, and considerable time. Furthermore, peak detection, integration, and identification in chromatograms can be automated by artificial intelligence (AI) methods like machine learning and deep learning, allowing for quicker and more precise analysis of complicated datasets, resulting in the identification of compounds and the comprehension of complex reactions more quickly and creatively. From an economic perspective, these developments promote sustainable analytical chemistry and effective resource recovery. Moreover, AI can increase productivity and reduce the possibility of human error by automating chromatographic analysis. Additionally, AI has played a key role in enhanced analysis of complicated spectra in fields like spectroscopy and chromatography, as well as in handling heterogeneous data. This mini review discusses recent advancements in artificial intelligence and machine learning (ML) that enable scientists to address complex analytical challenges more effectively. It highlights the growing application of these technologies in chromatographic predictions, particularly in liquid chromatography method development. The present review further examines key AI-driven areas, including automated method development, retention time prediction, peak deconvolution, predictive maintenance, and intelligent data processing.

Introduction Generative AI legal assistants rely on users to describe events, evidence, and transaction histories, yet the same accounts may contain private information that is unnecessary for legal guidance. Empathetic language may affect how selectively users decide what to provide. Methods A one-factor between-subjects online survey experiment on Wenjuanxing randomly assigned 360 participants to rational, mildly empathetic, or highly empathetic AI legal responses (n = 120 per condition). Participants completed 1-5 Likert-type measures of parasocial response, privacy boundary judgment, and over-disclosure intention, together with related relational measures, and then answered an open-ended disclosure task. Results The empathy manipulation was successful, F (2,357) = 524.170, p < 0.001, and η 2 = 0.746. Stronger empathetic responses increased parasocial response (η 2 = 0.428), reduced privacy boundary judgment (η 2 = 0.242), and increased over-disclosure intention (η 2 = 0.406). The coded non-essential disclosure score rose from 0.994 in the rational condition to 6.132 in the highly empathetic condition, F (2,357) = 170.795, p < 0.001, and η 2 = 0.489. Necessary case facts remained stable, F (2,357) = 0.245, p = 0.783. Bootstrap analysis yielded an indirect effect through parasocial response of 0.214, 95% CI [0.151, 0.283], and a sequential indirect effect through parasocial response and privacy boundary judgment of 0.063, 95% CI [0.033, 0.098]. Discussion Within this consumer-dispute scenario, stronger empathetic cues reduced users' selectivity about which information was appropriate to provide. Data-minimization prompts and evidence-oriented questioning may help retain limited emotional support without encouraging unnecessary disclosure.

documents.abstract: Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-based immunotherapy has transformed cancer treatment by enabling engineered immune cells to selectively recognize and eliminate malignant targets, with CAR-T cells establishing the first major clinical success in this field. However, severe associated toxicities, logistical complexities of autologous manufacturing, and high rates of antigen-loss relapse have accelerated the development of alternative effector platforms such as CAR-NK cells. CAR-NK cells combine antigen-directed cytotoxicity with the innate antitumor functions of natural killer cells, offering a potentially safer and more readily available off-the-shelf therapeutic strategy. Nevertheless, the clinical efficacy of CAR-NK therapy is constrained by key biological and translational hurdles: brief in vivo persistence, inadequate trafficking and solid tumor infiltration, severe susceptibility to tumor microenvironment-mediated immunosuppression, and antigen escape driven by tumor heterogeneity. These biological constraints are compounded by technical bottlenecks, including cell source variability, limited large-scale expansion capacity, ex vivo functional exhaustion, and an absence of standardized manufacturing protocols. To address these multi-faceted barriers, recent advances in genome engineering, systems biology, and computational modeling provide promising routes forward. Given that prolonged exposure to immunosuppressive niches induces functional impairment, genome-editing strategies targeting inhibitory checkpoints and persistence programs are crucial; however, enhancing persistence requires stringent safeguards to mitigate toxicity risks from constitutive signaling or genomic instability. Thus, engineering next-generation CAR-NK cells necessitates balancing extended longevity, potent cytotoxicity, and safety. Multiomics approaches facilitate deeper characterization of CAR-NK functional states and tumor–immune interactions, whereas artificial intelligence–guided engineering integrates high-dimensional biological and manufacturing data to optimize receptor design, predict therapeutic performance, and accelerate translational workflows. Collectively, these innovations support a paradigm shift toward programmable CAR-NK cells that can dynamically sense, adapt, and respond to tumor evolution, driving the transition toward autonomous, highly scalable, and precisely controllable cellular immunotherapies in precision oncology.

This thesis analyzes the didactic potential of using interactive and innovative pedagogical technologies to enhance students’ learning activity, cognitive engagement, educational motivation, and participation in collaborative activities within differentiated instruction. Particular attention is paid to adapting interactive methods to differences in students’ levels of knowledge, interests, pace of learning, and individual educational needs. The role of problem-based learning, project-based learning, gamification, cooperative learning, the flipped classroom model, multimedia tools, and other innovative approaches in differentiated instruction is examined.

Generative AI performance disparities can exclude minority-language speakers from digital participation. Drawing on Fricker’s epistemic-injustice framework, we examined five Chinese minority languages using four-way causal mediation decomposition, intersectional analysis, and participatory evaluation. Under the measured mediators and model specification, non-PIE components accounted for an average of 67.5% of observed disparities. Tibetan speech recognition yielded a 43.9% word error rate (WER) for elderly speakers using religious and dialectal language, 6.9 percentage points above the main-effects additive reference. Community evaluation prioritized religious sensitivity, while threshold rules identified culturally salient failures missed by linear weighting. CAML-LLM, integrating cultural knowledge graphs, multimodal alignment, and community-weighted training, reduced WER from 31.2% to 22.7% and improved cultural appropriateness by 22.5%. These findings characterize model-dependent disparities and demonstrate that participatory system design can improve minority-language performance within the evaluated settings.

documents.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) in library offers a transformative opportunity to enhance service delivery amidst persistent staffing and funding deficits. However, this technological shift creates tension regarding ethical governance, data privacy, and cultural representation. This study investigated the ethical dimensions and operational usage of AI for service delivery in Nigerian academic libraries, with policy frameworks, algorithmic justice, data privacy, and technological equity. The study adopted a descriptive survey research design. The population comprised 8,323 certified librarians in Nigeria, from which a sample size of 368 was selected using a convenience/purposive sampling technique. Data collection was executed using a validated self-structured 5-point Likert scale questionnaire administered during the EDO 2025 Nigerian Library Association (NLA) Conference. A total of 318 valid copies were retrieved, yielding an 86.4% response rate. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, including frequency counts, percentages, mean, and standard deviation. The results revealed that while librarians demonstrate a high overall level of ethical awareness and a desire for structural policy frameworks (M = 3.64), their specific practical awareness regarding daily data privacy and intellectual property implications remains high (M = 3.79). Result showed that current library professional ethics are moderate (M=3.36) to regulate AI adoption. Furthermore, respondents reported a moderately critical level of algorithmic bias moderate (M=3.10), strongly indicating that current Western-centric AI systems marginalize local research, regional cultural contexts, and indigenous Nigerian languages. Concerns surrounding data privacy, cloud breaches, and third-party commercial data-mining also scored moderate (M=3.18), exposing the vulnerabilities of libraries operating with sub-baseline digital infrastructures. The study concluded that forcing AI adoption without context-responsive ethical governance exacerbates algorithmic injustice and risks compromising user trust. It is recommended that stakeholders co-design localized AI deployment policies, conduct rigorous pre-deployment algorithmic audits, and establish human-AI collaborative frameworks for patron confidentiality against aggressive data mining.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Algorithms now shape who gets diagnosed, who gets treated, and who gets overlooked, and too often they reproduce the very inequities medicine claims to fight. This chapter examines how bias enters clinical artificial intelligence and what it costs patients. Drawing on systematic reviews and real cases, it traces the mechanisms, training data that underrepresents minority populations, models that learn from unequal patterns of care, and proxies like health spending that mistake access for need, producing tools that score black patients as healthier than they are. It looks at race correction in kidney and other algorithms, uneven accuracy across racial groups in cardiovascular and imaging models, and the transparency gaps that let these flaws go unnoticed. Finally, it turns to solutions, explainable AI that lets clinicians interrogate algorithmic logic, guiding principles for fairer design, and the regulation, accountability, and physician vigilance required to ensure these systems advance justice rather than entrench disparity.

documents.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in education, but evidence on their performance comes mainly from high-resource languages. We evaluated five commercial LLMs in Kazakh in a zero-shot setting: sentiment classification on 300 class-balanced KazSAnDRA reviews and question answering (QA) on the same 300 randomly sampled KazQAD questions with and without the gold supporting passage. Exact McNemar tests with Holm correction found no significant pairwise differences on sentiment classification, one with supporting context, and nine without context under the Containment criterion. For OpenAI and Anthropic, the higher-tier model had a larger advantage over its lower-tier counterpart when the supporting passage was removed (tier-by-regime interaction: OR = 1.92, 95% CI [1.52, 2.43]). Closed-book scores were affected by output format, inflectional morphology, and answer length. Human evaluation of 500 QA responses showed that string-based metrics substantially underestimated closed-book accuracy (0.55 by human judgement versus 0.26 by Containment). Under human judgement, the three higher-scoring models did not differ significantly from one another. Access to a relevant passage narrowed differences between models, although this oracle-context condition did not test a retrieval system. These findings support task-specific evaluation of Kazakh-language educational assistants and the use of answer-matching criteria checked against human judgement.

Purpose This study aims to develop and evaluate an explainable machine-learning framework to anticipate county-level high recovery burden from natural disasters one year ahead using only public administrative and social-vulnerability data. Its substantive aim is to help built-environment decision makers shift from reactive post-event allocation to earlier, place-based prioritization of recovery and mitigation effort. Design/methodology/approach A county-year panel was assembled for 3,042 US counties over 2014–2022 by combining FEMA Disaster Declarations Summaries with county-level CDC/ATSDR social vulnerability index data. The outcome was a high-burden county-year, defined as repeated county-level declarations involving public assistance and/or hazard mitigation programme activity. Class-weighted logistic regression, random forest and XGBoost were benchmarked using a temporally ordered train-validation-test split. SHAP values and model coefficients were used to interpret predictive drivers. Findings The benchmark produced a moderate but decision-relevant predictive signal. Class-weighted logistic regression achieved the strongest out-of-sample performance on the hold-out period (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve 0.626; area under the precision–recall curve 0.140; F1-score 0.262) and outperformed the more flexible tree-based models. Across models, stronger prior programme burden, recent major declarations, population size, mobile-home prevalence and social vulnerability were associated with higher next-year burden. Research limitations/implications The dependent variable is an administrative proxy for recovery burden rather than a direct measure of physical loss, repair cost or household recovery outcomes. The empirical setting is the USA; transfer to other countries should therefore be treated as conceptual and methodological rather than statistical. Practical implications The framework offers a transparent annual screening tool for local governments, regional planning bodies and emergency-management agencies seeking to identify counties likely to face elevated recovery pressure. Social implications Because it relies on public tabular data rather than expensive proprietary inputs, it is potentially transferable to resource-constrained settings that need interpretable anticipatory analytics. Originality/value The paper contributes a reproducible public-data pipeline that links explainable artificial intelligence to disaster-resilience planning in the built environment. It also responds to the journal’s growing interest in technology-enabled resilience by showing that interpretable models, rather than only complex algorithms, can support forward-looking preparedness and recovery prioritization.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has been widely adopted in corporate innovation activities, yet prior research has not reached a consensus on whether it is more conducive to incremental or radical innovation. For radical innovation, which depends on highly novel ideas, realizing the value of AI depends not only on whether AI is adopted but, more importantly, on whether employees can use it creatively to transcend established knowledge boundaries. Drawing on environmental dynamism and the exploration–exploitation perspective, this study develops a theoretical model linking leaders’ perceptions of environmental dynamism, employees’ AI use modes, leader temporal myopia, and employee radical creativity in the context of AI-enabled drug discovery. We distinguish leaders’ perceptions of environmental dynamism into perceived technological dynamism and perceived market dynamism, and employees’ AI use into exploratory and exploitative AI use. The model is tested using partial least squares structural equation modeling and three-wave matched survey data from 368 leader–employee dyads. The results show that leader-perceived technological dynamism is positively associated with employee exploratory AI use, whereas leader-perceived market dynamism is positively associated with employee exploitative AI use. Exploratory AI use is positively associated with employee radical creativity, whereas exploitative AI use is negatively associated with it. Leader temporal myopia weakens the positive conditional indirect relationship of technological dynamism with radical creativity through exploratory AI use and strengthens the negative conditional indirect relationship of market dynamism with radical creativity through exploitative AI use. By adopting a knowledge-activity perspective, this study reveals the differentiated relationships between AI use modes and radical creativity and further explains how perceptions of the external environment, leaders’ temporal orientation, and employees’ AI use behaviors are differentially related. The findings provide a theoretical basis and practical implications for helping firms engaged in AI-enabled drug discovery guide employees toward effective AI use and enhance radical creativity.

This article examines the extent to which private technology companies bear responsibility for respecting human rights, particularly freedom of expression, when governing social media content through artificial intelligence (AI), and how that responsibility relates to the legal obligations of States. It focuses on the rule-of-law complexities created by the interaction between territorially based public regulation and transnational platform governance. Through a comparative analysis of domestic law and platform practice, the article assesses how AI-mediated content moderation affects online expression. The revised analysis is limited to India, Bangladesh, Pakistan and Afghanistan as selected comparative cases; it distinguishes State duties from the corporate responsibility to respect human rights, and treats AI-mediated moderation as including automated detection, classification, recommendation, down-ranking, removal and account restrictions. It proposes a seven-element human-rights test for AI-mediated moderation: legality, legitimate aim, necessity, proportionality, transparency, procedural fairness and effective remedy.

documents.abstract: Abstract Synthetic tabular data generation plays a key role in alleviating data scarcity and privacy limitations in machine learning, especially in regulated domains such as finance and healthcare. While many existing methods focus on producing realistic and predictive tabular data, fairness is often not explicitly considered, leading to biased synthetic datasets. Recent approaches based on large language models (LLMs) further enhance data quality through natural language representations, which underscores the need for principled mechanisms that ensure fairness alongside predictive performance. To address this challenge, we propose SENNA, a framework that integrates disentangled semantic representations with LLM-based generation to jointly preserve utility and improve fairness. The framework separates task-relevant and task-independent information in the latent space and leverages these representations to guide generation and validation. Experimental results on three real-world datasets show that SENNA achieves competitive downstream performance, while substantially reducing both group-level disparities and individual-level inequality. We further evaluate the framework across multiple backbones, providing insights into fairness–utility trade-offs in LLM-based tabular data synthesis.

documents.abstract: Federated Artificial Intelligence of Things (AIoT) activity-recognition systems learn from decentralized wearable and smart-home records with potentially incorrect labels, non-IID client distributions, and unequal edge-device resources.Our objective is to improve downstream learning from these labels while limiting harmful corrections and respecting auditing, review, and communication budgets.FedCuraLM addresses this objective by converting sensor records into deterministic Semantic Evidence Cards, obtaining candidate-constrained small language model (SLM) assessments, and calibrating and combining them with task-model, prototype, and temporal evidence. Conflict-aware decisions retain observed labels, apply provisional soft corrections, request trusted review, or quarantine uncertain samples without overwriting annotations. Review-grounded reliability and communication-budgeted multi-prototype exchange support collaboration, while resource-aware scheduling assigns feasible SLM tiers across heterogeneous devices. Extensive evaluation on WISDM-W, WISDM-P, and CASAS using controlled symmetric, semantic-asymmetric, instance-dependent, and temporal-boundary corruption under varying client heterogeneity reveals that FedCuraLM significantly improves downstream performance over recent baselines and improves lower-tail client outcomes, audit precision, selective-correction safety, calibration, and communication efficiency. Edge-device measurements characterize latency, memory, and energy trade-offs. The findings position federated label curation as a semantic, statistical, communication, and systems problem.

Stacking task adapters on a frozen domain adapter is a common approach for modular specialization of large language models, usually justified by knowledge injection; whether the surface-form graders standard in this setting can measure such specialization validly has remained unexamined. Two challenges follow: isolating the domain layer’s marginal contribution under identical task training, and determining whether measured differences reflect competence or output form. In this work, both are addressed with a matched-arm DoRA ablation on a frozen Qwen 3.5 9B hybrid: a 242 M-parameter domain expert is trained on a licensed 27.8 M-token corpus, and byte-identical task adapters are trained flat, stacked (DFE-stacking), and jointly across three tasks and five conditions, with the key extraction pair replicated at a second training seed; every grader is audited by per-item failure classification and a dual-rater blind human re-grade with consensus adjudication. The principal finding is that fine-tuning shifts output form before competence: stacking yields no seen-task benefit; an apparent generalization collapse on an unseen schema reduces to a single, highly seed-stable formatting coercion that the domain layer dampens and task-mixture training eliminates, and most automated keyword-grading failures prove to be correct paraphrases, leaving no genuine capability loss detected on any instrument. Because such style drift is induced by the training condition itself, surface-sensitive grader error becomes bias aligned with experimental arms rather than noise. Three additional experiments extend the findings: the coercion replicates on Llama 3.1 8B (60% vs. 19% untuned); a pre-registered 240-item formatting-perturbation battery across four further unseen schemas and eight conventions reveals fine-tuned conditions ranking lowest under strict grading yet highest under format-normalized grading; and a matched-compute wrong-domain control shows the domain layer’s coercion dampening to be generic substrate regularization, while value integrity under the induced drift tracked the substrate’s domain. The principal contribution lies in the identification and quantification of this confound: surface-form evaluation of adapter specialization is structurally confounded, and per-item audits of the type released herein are a necessary component of specialization studies.

One of the most prevalent workplace-related musculoskeletal disorders is Carpal Tunnel Syndrome (CTS), which is caused by compression of the median nerve at the wrist due to prolonged improper wrist posture. Continuous monitoring of wrist posture is essential to prevent serious complications, including the need for surgery. Current monitoring methods are often limited by high cost and poor portability because they rely on expensive electronics, rigid sensors, or vision-based systems. Wearable, flexible sensing technologies have emerged as an attractive solution for early detection and prevention of musculoskeletal disorders, as well as for continuous health monitoring. This work presents a low-cost, wearable, flexible, silver-conductive ink-patterned paper patch for continuous wrist posture monitoring and identification of ergonomic factors associated with CTS. Silver nanoparticles were synthesised by a chemical reduction method owing to their high electrical conductivity and superior oxidation resistance compared with copper, and the silver conductive ink was formulated using suitable binders. The conductive ink pattern printed on a flexible paper substrate undergoes mechanical deformation during wrist movement, resulting in detectable variations in resistance that correlate with changes in wrist bending angle. An Arduino-based system continuously monitored the resistance variations using a threshold-based algorithm, while an HC-05 Bluetooth module and a custom MIT App Inventor application wirelessly transmitted the wrist posture status to a smartphone. Experimental evaluation demonstrated accurate real-time detection of wrist posture with successful wireless ergonomic feedback. The proposed paper-based wearable system provides a lightweight, flexible, and cost-effective solution for the early detection and warning of potentially risky wrist position associated with CTS in industrial workers and computer users.

documents.abstract: Contamination of water by microbial pathogens and chemical pollutants is a serious threat to human health, ecosystems, and industries globally. Conventional water quality surveillance techniques, like lab-based tests, have problems like delays, high cost, and complicated sample preparation, which act as a hindrance to serving real-time information. Fluorescent and optical sensors are an encouraging way out of such constraints, as they can be used to detect waterborne contaminants in real time and in situ. These are sensitive sensors, which can detect even low traces of contaminants and can provide quick data, which is vital in making prompt intervention during water treatment and in protecting human health. Fluorescent sensors are designed to monitor the fluorescent characteristics of the contaminants, whereas optical sensors are designed to monitor the interactions of light, including absorption, scattering, or reflection. They are especially applicable in on-site monitoring in a wide variety of conditions, such as remote or emergency situations, due to their portability and cost-effectiveness. Although they have their advantages, there are challenges that include interference by other substances, sensitivity to environmental factors, and degradation of the sensor. Yet, the combination of the development of nanomaterials, artificial intelligence, and wireless technology has excessive opportunities to improve the performance and increase the scope of these sensors. This chapter discusses the concepts, uses, benefits, and drawbacks of fluorescent and optical sensors and the future of their use in transforming the world in its water-quality monitoring.

Abstract Drawing on the notion of workplace learning this study examines how academic development can design and facilitate team learning in the academic workplace to support co-constructive educational innovation. Based on a qualitative case study at a Swiss University of Teacher Education, it analyses a participatory initiative addressing generative artificial intelligence (genAI) in assessment. The staged process combined SWOT-based collective sense-making, a design sprint, selective project funding, and facilitated reflection during project development. Data consisted of process documentation and collaboratively generated written reflections, which were analysed and refined through iterative feedback and co-writing. The findings show how structured formats, shared artefacts, and deliberate facilitation enabled participants to make distributed expertise visible, develop shared problem understandings, form project teams, and move from exchange towards co-construction and coordinated experimentation. At the same time, public pitching, funding decisions, time pressures, and institutional constraints created tensions between collaboration and competition, openness and focus, and participation and decision-making. The study suggests that academic development can support educational innovation by acting as facilitator, trust-building broker, and co-learner. Its contribution lies in conceptualising participatory innovation processes as workplace-learning arrangements that connect emerging team-learning processes with local experimentation and wider institutional conversations, while recognising that organisational learning requires further institutional uptake.

documents.abstract: We propose Fractal Information AI (FIAI), a graph-based architecture for adaptive learning in which knowledge is represented as recursively organized information structures and learning actions are prioritized by validated information gain, uncertainty reduction, network propagation, and decision relevance. The framework originates from a fractal-tree interpretation in which branches carry information, knots encode rule families, and paths represent inferential relations. For artificial intelligence, the logical notion of formal provability is retained only where machine-checkable verification is available; in open-domain settings it is generalized to an evidence-validation or consistency gate. Each knowledge node carries an unresolved-state variable, provenance, verifier status, information-gain estimate, decision relevance, and propagation weights. A Learning Efficiency Metric (LEM) quantifies validated uncertainty reduction per available unresolved mass or, in cost-aware form, per unit acquisition/computation cost. Multiple agents exchange validated knowledge through bound coupling operators, allowing the study of knowledge hubs, bottlenecks, redundancy, and emergent collaborative structures. We derive deterministic and stochastic node dynamics, stability conditions for propagation, and bounds on cross-agent transfer. A reproducible numerical illustration with three interacting 20-node knowledge trees demonstrates LEM trajectories, decreasing unresolved mass, and node-level utility concentration. FIAI is presented as a testable architectural hypothesis rather than a demonstrated replacement for transformer, graph-neural, retrieval-augmented, or multi-agent systems. Its central empirical claim is that explicit knowledge-utility accounting can improve the allocation of learning and verification resources under fixed budgets.

The transition from petroleum-derived polymers to renewable materials requires biorefineries capable of managing the compositional variability and multiscale structure of lignocellulosic biomass. This conceptual narrative review examines fractal-inspired principles—including hierarchical organization, branching, modularity, and finite-range statistical self-similarity—as a design perspective for integrated biorefineries. Deterministic mathematical fractals are distinguished from statistical fractals and hierarchical engineered systems, and methods for characterizing scale-dependent surfaces, porous catalysts, and transport networks are reviewed. The coordinated valorization of cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin is then considered within an integrated biomass-to-chemicals framework for producing platform chemicals, functional materials, and polymer precursors. Petroleum crude-to-chemicals processing, including the S-OIL Shaheen Project, is discussed as a limited industrial benchmark for integrated fractionation, residue upgrading, and product diversification rather than as direct evidence of fractal engineering. An integrated framework is proposed in which fractal-inspired design provides the physical and organizational architecture, artificial intelligence supports characterization, prediction, optimization, and control, and Industry 5.0 provides the objectives of sustainability, resilience, and human-centered manufacturing. The framework remains conceptual. Its potential benefits must be evaluated through transport modeling, mass and energy balances, process simulation, experimental comparison, techno-economic analysis, and life-cycle assessment.

Background: Dental caries is the most prevalent noncommunicable disease worldwide. Within the DCIEH framework it is a dysbiosis of the dental biofilm microbiome that is regulated by biology, modulated by behavior and conditioned by the environment. It is also a trans-complex disease whose outcome emerges from the interaction of biological, behavioral and socio-environmental factors. Behavioral sciences offer mature theories to explain and change oral health behaviors, but a persistent gap separates these theories from routine chairside care. In 2024 we proposed ELIGE/CHOOSE, a theoretical framework that integrates Social Cognitive Theory (SCT) and the Capability-Opportunity-Motivation-Behavior (COM-B) model into three clinical phases: Identify, Articulate and Plan.Objective: To report the systematic development of ELIGE AI, a clinical decision support tool that operationalizes the ELIGE/CHOOSE framework through an evidence-based, author-designed deterministic algorithm combined with a large language model (LLM).Methods: Development was guided by the Medical Research Council framework for complex interventions, the ORBIT model and the IDEAS framework for digital behavior change interventions. Reporting draws on TIDieR, DECIDE-AI and TRIPOD-LLM. Development proceeded in five phases: (1) theoretical integration of SCT, COM-B, the Transtheoretical Model, the Health Action Process Approach, motivational interviewing and Intervention Mapping; (2) translation into a stepwise clinical protocol; (3) formalization of the first author's clinical reasoning as an explicit decision algorithm, with every rule traceable to theory or evidence; (4) integration of an LLM restricted to bounded language tasks; and (5) iterative build-and-refine cycles across versions informed by clinical use.Results: ELIGE AI (v3.9) is a web application with seven screens across the three ELIGE/CHOOSE phases plus a follow-up module. In about 20 to 25 minutes it produces a specified behavior, a principal COM-B determinant with a displayed rationale, a graded goal ladder, Behaviour Change Technique Taxonomy v1 techniques matched to the determinant, rule-based referrals and personalized patient materials. At follow-up it re-measures the same constructs, behavior frequency and dental caries risk, and recommends the next step on the same behavioral route. The algorithm makes every clinical decision; the LLM only drafts and classifies; the clinician validates and can override every output.Conclusions: ELIGE AI shows how a published behavioral framework and its author's clinical reasoning can be encoded as a transparent algorithm and safely combined with generative AI. The tool now enters a three-stage evaluation of usability, feasibility and validity, and efficacy on dental caries outcomes.

documents.abstract: Large language models and the agents built on them can reach the same outcome through different internal computations, reasoning trajectories, and system-level policies. Existing reviews typically treat mechanistic interpretability, reasoning, agent architectures, and safety separately, leaving no common framework for analyzing how a system represents alternatives, evaluates them, commits to one, executes it, and revises that choice. This article presents a structured review and a faceted taxonomy of decision making and strategy selection in LLMs and LLM-based agents. The framework separates system locus—model, harness, or their tested interaction—from temporal scope—a single forward pass or call, a reasoning episode, or an agent trajectory—and decomposes decision making into six functional stages from state representation to update or termination. Five claim-specific evidential relations distinguish behavioral observation, representation decoding, causal influence, controlled manipulation, and mechanistic explanation, while robustness is assessed separately across prompts, tasks, models, harness configurations, and independent replication. Across the literature, evidence is strongest for local mechanisms within individual model calls and substantially weaker for persistent strategies across agent trajectories. The central unresolved gap is cross-scope continuity: few studies follow the same decision variable from internal representation through commitment, executed action, and subsequent feedback. A July 2026 agent-security incident is used to illustrate how the framework converts observed coordination and constraint circumvention into testable causal hypotheses.

Digital technologies are reshaping how small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) in emerging economies respond to environmental pressure, yet two questions remain open. Research linking digital skilling to sustainability has largely tested direct effects without tracing the behavioral pathway such an effect would have to travel, and attitudes toward artificial intelligence have rarely been examined as a condition governing whether green entrepreneurial activity converts into performance. This study addresses both. Integrating the Theory of Planned Behavior, Diffusion of Innovations Theory, and Contingency Theory into a single explanatory sequence, it models climate entrepreneurship (CE), green entrepreneurial behavior (GEB), and green entrepreneurial intention (GEI) as the mechanisms linking digital entrepreneurial education and training (DEET) to sustainable environmental performance (SEP) and sustainable organizational performance (SOP), with commitment to the environment (CTE) and attitude toward artificial intelligence (ATAI) as boundary conditions. Survey data from 648 Pakistani SMEs are analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling, with a random forest robustness check confirming that the modelled relationships are linear and compensatory. DEET directly predicts organizational performance but has no significant direct effect on environmental performance; its environmental influence is transmitted entirely through the three behavioral mechanisms. Environmental commitment and favorable attitudes toward artificial intelligence each strengthen the conversion of green entrepreneurship into sustainability outcomes, though the interaction effects are modest in magnitude. The findings suggest that digital skilling initiatives are unlikely to yield environmental returns unless paired with entrepreneurial agency and technological openness, with implications for the sequencing of digital and AI-readiness policy in resource-constrained economies.

This paper presents the evolving concept of authorship in music creation as algorithmic and artificial intelligence systems impact the musical market. Based on Philip Galanter's definition of generative art, the paper discusses about the authorship of music in different senerios: when it is generated by tools like Nyquist or AI models such as Suno. The argument is structured around three distinct ways of human-machine interaction: human-led creation where computers are used as instruments; human-guided creation, where algorithms are restricted to a predetermined range of randomness; and human-crafted prompts, where AI generates the music completely. Following the analysis of these cases and some complex instances, this paper concludes that authorship is decided by the location of creativity and intentionality rather than a fixed attribute. The analysis reveals that authorship belongs to different subjects accordingly to different methods humans used to use generative tools: following the primary source of meaning contribution. Ultimately, the paper argues that the central issue may not be the authorship itself, but the human need for music to serve as a bridge for shared meaning and emotional connection.

This paper examines how ride-hailing and delivery workers in Indonesia and the Philippines, as active technology actors, navigate and contest digital infrastructures that govern their labor. In contexts marked by platform dependency and labor insecurity, we move beyond discrete accounts of compliance and resistance to argue that worker agency lies in the capacity to move fluidly along a continuum of optimization and subversion practices. Drawing on 142 worker interviews, we find that these practices are embedded in the shifting dynamics of permissibility on platforms, workers’ familiarity with their apps, and the everyday ethical positioning of workers who continually balance the need to maintain access to the platform with efforts to improve pay and conditions. This dynamic exposes a paradox: platforms rely on workers’ ingenuity to patch systemic gaps and sustain operations even as they attempt to constrain it. By allowing oscillation between optimization and subversion, platforms defuse frustration, manage precarity, and secure their own endurance. Ultimately, this paper demonstrates how survival-driven adaptations both express worker agency and coshape platform capitalism from below—showing that platform arrangements are engineered from above yet are continually sustained, challenged, and reshaped through workers’ everyday practice.

Generative artificial intelligence can produce menus, recipes, shopping lists, and dietary explanations that appear individualized and clinically informed. Fluency alone, however, provides little evidence of nutritional accuracy, safety, feasibility, or benefit. We propose VALID-Diet, a staged framework for evaluating systems that generate actionable dietary recommendations as sociotechnical interventions. Its domains are Verification of nutritional targets and composition; Adversarial safety and boundary testing; Linkage between user inputs and recommendation changes; Implementation feasibility and inclusion; and Documentation, versioning, and reproducibility. Stage 0 defines intended use, input integrity, and a structured risk profile based on harm severity, exposure, autonomy, reversibility, and enforceable oversight. Stage 1 separates target validity, menu achievement, and arithmetic agreement and, for integrated systems, tests retrieval, calculation, and generation as distinct components. Stage 2 evaluates safety, substantive personalization, feasibility, and inclusion using pre-specified case blueprints. Stage 3 evaluates human oversight, workflow utility, and prospective outcomes only after earlier gates are passed. A retrospective worked application to a published retrieval-augmented personalized-nutrition system illustrates risk assignment and progression decisions. VALID-Diet is not a regulatory standard or consensus guideline; it is a testable proposal intended to align research claims with evidentiary strength.

documents.abstract: Abstract In the last four decades, the transmission of a live surgical operation to a remote audience has evolved from closed-circuit educational broadcast into a fully remote, robot-assisted surgery performed across different continents. This review maps that journey systematically, defining a six-rung Digital Surgical Spectrum — from passive live broadcast to artificial-intelligence-augmented autonomous surgery — grounding each stage in published clinical evidence across multiple surgical domains. We demonstrate that each rung of this spectrum is no longer theoretical. Live broadcasts have reached audiences across multiple countries. Tele-proctoring was validated at scale during the COVID-19 pandemic, and tele-mentoring has been shown in systematic review to produce a safety and efficacy profile broadly comparable to on-site supervision. True remote tele-surgery has been accomplished over distances exceeding 8,000 km with latencies well within established procedure specific safety thresholds. We also present a case timeline and an Institutional Readiness Framework specifying the technical, regulatory, and other prerequisites for each rung, organized visually as a Digital Surgical Spectrum. Importantly, nuances such as the performance paradox of observed surgery, consent frameworks, cybersecurity risk, regulatory fragmentation, and the threat of entrenching rather than correcting global surgical inequity are examined. As the field advances, the growth of tele-surgical technologies will depend on international regulatory harmonization and equity-centered deployment, supported by prospective multi-specialty outcome registries.

The integration of generative artificial intelligence into contemporary artistic practices requires reconsidering creativity, authorship, and originality, transforming relationships between artist, tool, and artwork. Unlike conventional digital technologies, which execute operations defined by creators, generative systems exhibit operational autonomy, producing partly unpredictable visual configurations. This raises questions about algorithmic intervention and the possibility of attributing co-authorship to artificial intelligence systems. This article examines the relationship between human creators and generative technologies through computational creativity, distributed authorship, and philosophical perspectives on nonhuman agency. It distinguishes systems’ operational autonomy from artists’ intentional autonomy, arguing that algorithmic participation does not necessarily imply creative subjectivity comparable to human experience. It also examines the aesthetic and conceptual implications of human–machine collaboration and the reorganisation of artistic practices through generation, selection, interpretation, and post-production. The study argues that generative artificial intelligence reconfigures human authorship, shifting creative activity from direct execution toward intention formulation, system configuration, and critical evaluation. Artists therefore retain a decisive role in directing the process and taking responsibility for its artistic outcomes. Algorithmic co-authorship serves as a conceptual tool for understanding these emerging production relationships, without implying legal authorship or artificial consciousness.

This article examines the theoretical and methodological aspects of optimizing treasury business processes through artificial intelligence and machine learning technologies. It substantiates the need for treasury digitalization to move beyond converting processes into electronic form towards the intelligent use of data. The article proposes a decision-support mechanism based on analyzing digital process traces through Process Mining, identifying redundant and repetitive operations, intelligently automating standard low-risk operations, and generating forecasts using machine learning. The author develops G-TOP, a mechanism for the intelligent optimization of treasury business processes, and TIOI, the Treasury Intelligent Optimization Index, to evaluate its effectiveness. The research findings demonstrate that artificial intelligence should be used in treasury operations not as a substitute for human decision-making, but as a technology that improves the quality of decisions

documents.abstract: Gender research in vocational education has primarily examined women’s exclusion, while male students’ experiences of privilege and masculinity-related pressure remain underexplored. This study examined how male vocational students experienced gender-based privilege, encountered psychological and pedagogical burdens, and interpreted their relationship during manufacturing internships. The study employed a qualitative design informed by a constructivist–interpretivist paradigm and Masculinity Studies, particularly Connell’s relational approach to masculinities. The study analyzed semi-structured interviews with 61 male students from two vocational secondary schools in Bekasi, Indonesia, using reflexive thematic analysis. Participants reported that gendered expectations associating men with strength, readiness, courage, and independence facilitated early access to core technical tasks, supervisory trust, and valuable learning opportunities. The same expectations intensified performance demands, physical workloads, risk exposure, restricted help-seeking, and limited pedagogical support. Participants interpreted this position through normalization, ambivalence, and critical reflection. Some proposed competency-based task allocation, equitable supervision, and safer learning environments. The study introduces conditional access privilege as a gendered position in which access to valuable technical learning resources must be maintained through masculine performance, generating psychological pressure and pedagogical vulnerability. The findings support internship practices that separate competency assessment, task allocation, supervision, and learning support from gendered expectations.
