documents.abstract: Early and accurate detection of pea diseases is essential for reducing crop losses and supporting precision agriculture. Although deep learning methods have shown good performance in plant disease classification, CNN-based models may have limitations in learning long-range relationships and detailed disease features. In this study, an explainable transformer-based framework, named PEAS-DeiT, is proposed for automated pea leaf disease classification. The proposed approach integrates a multi-scale spatial attention mechanism into the Data-efficient Image Transformer (DeiT) architecture to enhance the representation of disease-related visual features. A unified pea leaf disease dataset (UPLDD) was constructed by combining multiple publicly available datasets, covering six classes, including five disease categories and healthy samples. The proposed model was evaluated against CNN-based and transformer-based architectures using five-fold cross-validation. Furthermore, explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) analysis was performed to investigate the regions contributing to model predictions. Experimental results demonstrate that PEAS-DeiT achieved an accuracy of 93.11%, showing competitive performance compared with the evaluated CNN and transformer-based models. The gradient-based saliency analysis also revealed localized response patterns in several evaluated samples, providing qualitative insight into the image regions contributing to model predictions. Statistical analyses were conducted to evaluate the performance differences among the compared models. These findings indicate that PEAS-DeiT provides a competitive approach for pea leaf disease classification within the evaluated experimental setting.
topics: Industrial Vision Systems and Defect Detection

documents.abstract: Micro, small, and medium enterprises require practical digital marketing skills to produce attractive and consistent promotional content. This program aimed to strengthen the digital marketing capacity of 30 food and beverage MSMEs in Bojongloa Kaler District, Bandung City, through Generative Artificial Intelligence-based training and mentoring. Activities were implemented through needs identification, material and instrument preparation, interactive training, guided practice, mentoring, evaluation, and follow-up support. The training covered an introduction to GenAI, prompt engineering, caption writing, product descriptions, content ideas, promotional calendars, and simple digital design. Evaluation results showed that participants' average understanding increased from 54.2% in the pre-test to 96.4% in the post-test, representing a 42.2 percentage-point improvement. Participants produced reusable outputs, including captions, product descriptions, prompt templates, content calendars, and digital promotional materials. Although long-term sales and social media performance were not measured, these outputs provide a foundation for future monitoring and independent content production.

The rapid growth of the digital economy has opened vast opportunities through gig economy platforms, yet high school students and teachers often lack the digital literacy and skills needed to capitalize on these prospects productively. This community service program aimed to empower the economic potential of students and teachers at SMA IRA Medan by delivering education and technical training on digital freelance platforms integrated with Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Deep Learning tools. The methodology comprised three main stages: pre-implementation (need analysis, module synthesis, and institutional coordination), implementation (interactive seminar, live demonstration of AI tools, and hands-on portfolio creation workshops), and evaluation (pre-test/post-test analysis and mentoring). The activity took place at SMA IRA Medan on September 30, 2026, involving 40 participants consisting of students and teachers. The results demonstrated a significant increase in participant understanding, rising from an average of 23.1% in the pre-test to 88.8% in the post-test, an increase of 65.7%. Furthermore, 87.5% of participants successfully created active profiles and digital portfolios on platforms such as Sribulancer and Projects.co.id. This initiative successfully fostered a digital entrepreneurship mindset, equipping students and teachers with monetizable skills to support sustainable economic independence.

The rapid development of digital technology requires young people to utilize technology creatively and productively. This community service program aimed to strengthen students’ digital literacy through an introduction to information technology, Canva training, and the use of artificial intelligence (AI) at Pesantren Madani Sungai Alam. The program involved 20 students and was conducted on August 18 and 20, 2026, using a practice-based training approach consisting of material presentation, demonstration, hands-on practice, work appreciation, and mentoring. Program evaluation was carried out descriptively through direct observation and assessment of participants' practical work. The results demonstrated that participants gained practical experience in utilizing technology, Canva, and AI tools to develop creative ideas and produce digital content. This program establishes a foundational skill set that can be further enhanced through sustainable mentoring.

Citizens' social media posts can provide rapid, complementary situational information during emerging wildfires, alongside conventional sensing and official reporting. For Greek, no annotated wildfire corpus or end-to-end pipeline existed, and most systems stop at binary detection or depend on geotags. We present an end-to-end Greek-language NLP pipeline, a research prototype that turns keyword-retrieved, unlabeled X posts into a geolocated, near-real-time wildfire map: it detects active fires, types them as wildland, urban, or mixed, resolves toponyms, and clusters reports into incidents. On 3,277 manually annotated posts from two fire seasons, to our knowledge the first publicly released, agreement-audited Greek wildfire corpus, fine-tuned transformers reached F2 = 0.911 for detection and macro-F1 = 0.874 for fire type, outperforming classical baselines and, under the tested prompting conditions, two large language models, faster and at zero API cost. On a chronological hold-out of the unseen 2025 season, detection retains F2 = 0.850 (classification recall 0.907); fire-type classification degrades more (macro-F1 0.769 ± 0.085). Spatiotemporal toponym disambiguation raised geocoding accuracy from 54.68% to 80.58% (p < 0.001); a repeatability test revealed gazetteer drift. In a retrospective replay of 12 August 2024 posts, it resolved hundreds of reports of an Attica wildfire into one incident cluster, complementing emergency calls.

As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes increasingly integrated into the workplace, the risk that occupations will be replaced by AI has received widespread attention. Nevertheless, the underlying mechanisms linking AI-induced occupational replacement risk perception to individual withdrawal behaviors remain underexplored. Taking identity threat as an explanatory lens, this study integrates Identity Threat Theory (ITT) and Technology Threat Avoidance Theory (TTAT) to investigate the effect of occupational replacement risk perception on employee withdrawal behavior, with professional identity, work meaningfulness, and job insecurity serving as mediators and technological self-efficacy as a moderator. Two studies were conducted to test the theoretical model developed in this research. Study 1 developed and validated the AI-induced occupational replacement risk perception scale. Study 2 employed a three-wave time-lagged survey design to test the hypotheses. The results show that occupational replacement risk perception is positively associated with withdrawal behavior through decreased professional identity and work meaningfulness as well as increased job insecurity. Furthermore, these indirect effects are weaker among employees with higher technological self-efficacy. By illuminating the identity-threat mechanism that links AI-induced occupational replacement risk perception to employee behavior, this study opens the black box of how AI shapes employee responses, and it concludes with a discussion of the theoretical contributions and practical implications of these findings.

Abstract The widespread adoption of large language models has increased the need to distinguish human-authored text from AI-generated content, including cases in which generated text is subsequently rewritten or paraphrased. In practice, many detectors output only a single AI-likelihood score or percentage, offering limited transparency and little indication of whether a passage appears directly AI-written (AIW) or AI-rewritten (AIR). This study presents an agentic detection framework for two connected tasks: binary provenance detection (Human versus AI) and conditional subtype detection (AIW versus AIR). The dataset combined the Human-ChatGPT Comparison Corpus (HC3) and the ai-text-detection-pile with 4,348 pre-generated AIR records produced by a single GPT-based rewriting workflow. The proposed Qwen–LangGraph AI agent was compared to a HashingVectorizer–TF-IDF–SGD classifier, DeBERTa-v3-xsmall, and ELECTRA-small. On the binary test set, DeBERTa-v3-xsmall achieved the best discrimination (99.4995% accuracy and 99.9911% AUROC), whereas the agent achieved 98.8816% accuracy and 99.9187% AUROC. On the AI-only test set (10,769 AIW; 1,274 AIR), the agent obtained the highest threshold-based accuracy (96.7367%), macro-F1 (90.0357%), and AIR F1 (81.8643%), but its AUROC (83.2507%) and AUPR (79.7336%) were lower than those of the DeBERTa-v3-xsmall and ELECTRA-small transformers. Paired DeLong and McNemar analyses with Holm correction showed that the agent improved threshold-based AIR performance over the lexical baseline. Interpretability was operationalised through lexical weights, linguistic and out-of-distribution diagnostics, sentence-level indicators, and route traces. The findings support the use of AI as decision support, not as automated proof of plagiarism or misconduct.

(1) Background: The aim of this study was to analyze how teacher trainees and teachers relate to Artificial Intelligence (AI) in education across socio-emotional, attitudinal, competency-based, and ethical dimensions, considering the influence of personal, academic, and professional variables. The study was conceptually framed by the UNESCO AI Competency Framework for Teachers (AI CFT), complemented by DigCompEdu as a broader reference for teacher digital competence. (2) Methods: A quantitative, non-experimental, descriptive, cross-sectional design was developed with a sample of 1292 participants from Andalusia, consisting mainly of university students, along with teachers. The ACISE-IA scale, consisting of 39 items developed by Serrano-García et al. (2026), was used for data collection. (3) Results: The results showed that age and teaching experience are negatively associated with favorable attitudes and digital competence, while academic performance is positively related to greater openness, critical reflection, and perception of competence. Likewise, significant differences were identified according to the branch of knowledge, employment status, and academic year, with more positive assessments among students and in social science areas. (4) Conclusions: Overall, the findings show that the relationship with AI is not homogeneous, but rather modulated by educational and professional trajectories, underscoring the need to design flexible teacher training models that integrate technological development with pedagogical, emotional, and ethical reflection. These findings also contribute to educational sustainability by highlighting the importance of developing teacher training strategies that support the responsible and sustained integration of AI into educational systems.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming healthcare by enabling integration of genomic sequencing, wearable sensor streams, electronic health records, and environmental exposure data into predictive and preventive clinical systems. These advances support a transition from reactive treatment toward individualized precision health while simultaneously strengthening population-level analytics and public health decision making. Polygenic risk modeling, pharmacogenomics, real-world evidence platforms, and learning health systems illustrate how multimodal biomedical data infrastructures can improve early detection, treatment selection, and disease forecasting. However, these innovations introduce challenges involving algorithmic bias, privacy governance, interoperability, and equitable access to emerging technologies. Responsible deployment of large-scale health data requires transparency, regulatory oversight, and inclusive datasets that reflect diverse populations. The future of medicine will depend on balancing personalization with fairness while ensuring that AI-driven healthcare improves outcomes not only for individuals but also for entire communities through precision public health strategies.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Abstract—Physical Artificial Intelligence (Physical AI) represents a transformative frontier in autonomous cyber-physical robotics, shifting machine intelligence from disembodied algorithmic computation into dynamical systems that perceive, reason, and actuate directly within the physical world. While pure reinforcement learning (RL) and kinematic motion planners excel in controlled, isolated environments, deploying high-degree-of-freedom (DoF) bipedal humanoids and dexterous anthropomorphic hands in real-world unstructured settings introduces severe physical and computational bottlenecks: non-smooth contact mechanics, extreme sim-to-real transfer gaps, high-dimensional non-convex hybrid dynamics, and closed-loop motor bandwidth constraints. Differentiable Physics engines—which compute exact analytical state and contact gradients through forward simulation—alongside massively parallel GPU-accelerated domain randomization, establish a foundational computational methodology to bridge this chasm. This paper delivers an exhaustive, mathematically formal technical investigation and empirical benchmark of Physical AI for whole-body humanoid locomotion and dexterous tactile manipulation. We formalize the non-linear hybrid dynamical equations of underactuated bipedal contact, derive gradient backpropagation through Linear Complementarity Problem (LCP) friction cones, and model domain randomization over non-stationary physical distribution manifolds. Furthermore, we construct an empirical robotic evaluation testbed comprising full-scale bipedal humanoid platforms (Unitree H1, Fourier GR-1) and high-density optical tactile arrays (GelSight Svelte) evaluated across 800 challenging trials spanning uneven terrain locomotion, dynamic external impulse rejection, and blind in-hand object re-orientation. Our empirical findings demonstrate that differentiable physics-guided policy search achieves an 88.6% zero-shot sim-to-real locomotion transfer success rate, reducing training sample complexity by 4.2x over model-free PPO while bounding tracking error under 120 N external lateral impulses. Concurrently, high-frequency optical tactile feedback raises blind in-hand manipulation success by 54.2% over vision-only baselines. Finally, we formulate open challenges in non-rigid soft body contact differentiability, whole-body tactile-semantic foundation models, and real-time safety barrier certificates. Index Terms—Physical AI, Differentiable Physics, Sim-to-Real Transfer, Humanoid Locomotion, Whole-Body Control (WBC), Tactile Manipulation, Linear Complementarity Problem (LCP), Domain Randomization.

Abstract. Data-driven artificial intelligence (AI) weather models are increasingly positioned as alternatives or complements to physics-based numerical weather prediction (NWP) systems, yet systematic model evaluation studies that compare both paradigms under controlled experimental conditions remain limited. Here we present a structured model evaluation framework applying standardised verification metrics to assess a regional WRF configuration against three publicly available AI models – GraphCast, AIFS Single 1.0, and FuXi – over three high-impact flood events in Luxembourg and the Greater Region (2016, 2018, and 2021), comprising 90 simulation days and over 7300 matched forecast-observation pairs. The WRF model employs a three-dimensional variational (3D-VAR) data assimilation scheme ingesting GNSS Zenith Total Delay and conventional observations on a 6-hourly Rapid Update Cycle. All systems are initialised from ERA5 reanalysis to ensure consistent initial conditions. Categorical precipitation scores at the 1 mm threshold and continuous temperature metrics at surface stations serve as verification targets. Data assimilation measurably improves WRF's categorical precipitation skill (Critical Success Index: 0.306 to 0.341) while leaving near-surface temperature largely unchanged, demonstrating the value of the assimilation scheme. AIFS achieves the highest detection rate (POD 0.765) and net categorical skill (CSI 0.370), GraphCast and AIFS reduce temperature RMSE by ~10 % relative to assimilated WRF, and WRF alone reproduces the observed mesoscale precipitation structure of the catastrophic July 2021 flood. The per-event breakdown reveals no skill degradation for AI models on out-of-sample events, suggesting that meteorological regime rather than training-data overlap governs model performance. These results provide a replicable model evaluation methodology for benchmarking emerging data-driven NWP systems against observation-corrected regional models.

Objective: To map how exercise and physical-education research with university students has implemented assessment, subgroup targeting, individualized prescription, monitoring, feedback, and response-based adjustment, and to identify what is still required for a reproducible closed-loop precision-support system. Methods: This scoping review followed JBI guidance and the PRISMA extension for scoping reviews. PubMed, Scopus, and CINAHL Ultimate were searched on August 21, 2026, for English-language studies, supplemented by an existing 28-report full-text seed set. Eligible studies involved university students and evaluated an exercise, physical-education, fitness-testing, monitoring, or feedback component relevant to tailoring exercise support. A five-level framework was applied: standardized provision (level 0), subgroup targeting (level 1), assessment- or feedback-informed adaptation (level 2), individual prescription (level 3), and response-adaptive closed loop (level 4). Results: The searches and seed set identified 403 records; 358 unique records were screened, 48 reports were assessed in full text, and 30 studies entered the evidence map. Fifteen studies used standardized provision, three targeted a predefined subgroup, six implemented assessment, monitoring, or personalized feedback without a complete individual prescription, and six reported individual exercise prescriptions. No study fully specified a level-4 closed loop with prospective monitoring variables, decision thresholds, and reproducible rules for changing frequency, intensity, time, or type. Exercise programs improved selected fitness, body-composition, physical-activity, and mental-health outcomes, but effects were outcome-specific and heterogeneous. Wearables and mobile platforms made monitoring scalable, yet fixed goals, multicomponent designs, and limited use of monitored data for treatment decisions constrained personalization. Assessment feedback could also reduce competence and intrinsic motivation when interpreted negatively. Conclusions: The literature has progressed beyond uniform exercise delivery, but digital monitoring should not be equated with precision. A defensible university model requires an auditable chain from multidimensional assessment to stratification, FITT prescription, process monitoring, interpretable feedback, and threshold-based adjustment, alongside evaluation of safety, equity, adherence, teacher workload, and operational efficiency.

documents.abstract: Air pollution currently represents a significant environmental challenge with a direct impact on both public health and ecosystems. One of the aims of this paper is to predict the concentration of particulate matter PM10 and CO2 in the air using machine learning methods, specifically by employing various types of neural networks, including feedforward, convolutional, and recurrent models. The aim is also to compare the performance of these architectures in processing univariate time series with different temporal resolutions (monthly, hourly). The study uses real data from the Slovak Hydrometeorological Institute (SHMÚ) and modelled emissions from the EDGAR database. The models were trained, optimized, and evaluated using standard error metrics. The results showed that Conv1D models achieved the highest accuracy on hourly data of PM10, while feedforward architectures performed best on monthly national data of CO2. The findings confirm the potential of artificial intelligence methods as a tool for environmental monitoring and decision support in air quality protection. Opportunities for extending the models with meteorological variables and applying them in real-time warning systems are also discussed.

Smart electrical distribution networks are becoming more observable, automated, and data intensive, yet maintenance practice often remains dominated by periodic inspection or intervention after alarms and failures. This review develops a predictive maintenance framework that connects artificial intelligence and data analytics with the operational realities of distribution transformers, on-load tap changers, switchgear, circuit breakers, feeders, cables, substations, smart meters, and distributed-energy interfaces. The evidence base is restricted to peer-reviewed work published from 2020 to 2025 and is synthesized through a structured integrative review focused on data provenance, condition indicators, learning tasks, validation practice, interpretability, uncertainty, deployment constraints, and maintenance decision linkage. The review shows that useful predictive maintenance cannot be reduced to selecting a high-performing classifier. Reliable deployment requires a chain of asset-aware sensing, data-quality control, representation learning, anomaly detection, fault diagnosis, health forecasting, uncertainty estimation, consequence assessment, and human-governed maintenance orchestration. Deep learning and ensemble methods improve representation of nonlinear and temporal degradation, while digital twins can provide synchronized context, scenario testing, and traceability; however, scarce fault labels, changing operating regimes, class imbalance, fragmented semantics, cyber risk, and weak external validation remain major obstacles. A layered framework is therefore proposed in which analytical outputs are converted into risk-calibrated maintenance actions rather than isolated predictions. The framework emphasizes evidence quality, cross-asset generalization, explainable reasoning, model monitoring, and feedback from completed work orders. It provides a research and implementation architecture for moving smart distribution maintenance from condition visibility toward dependable, auditable, and economically meaningful predictive decision support.

Attrition among employees is one of the greatest concerns in the modern organization due to high expenses caused by recruiting new personnel, productivity losses, and reduction of corporate knowledge. In the research under consideration, there is a developed predictive modeling system intended to predict employee attrition and develop appropriate retention strategies. The proposed methodology uses complex machine learning techniques such as Random Forest, Gradient Boosting, and ensembles along with mechanisms of explainable artificial intelligence that provide transparency of the model and facilitate its application. By applying the IBM HR Analytics Employee Attrition dataset containing information about employees' features, the framework uses advanced techniques of preprocessing, class balancing, and feature engineering to take into account complex aspects of attrition. As a result of experiments, it is revealed that the ensemble model demonstrates better forecasting results compared to baseline models. The interpretation of results based on the SHAP technique shows that overtime, monthly income, length of service, and job satisfaction are the most important factors affecting attrition. Thus, the research provides an innovative approach that will help turn human resource management into proactive workforce planning.

Systematic review and meta-analysis of peer-reviewed studies (1 January 2020 to 23 September 2026) that develop or evaluate pretrained foundation models (DNA and RNA language models, single-cell foundation models, multimodal epigenomic models) for gene-regulatory prediction tasks. The review maps the evidence and pools within-study comparisons in which a foundation model and a task-specific deep-learning model trained from scratch are evaluated on the same test data. Reported according to PRISMA 2020 and PRISMA-S. The full protocol (amendment v0.3, 12 October 2026) is attached to this registration.

Abstract Objectives Silent vertebral fractures are common but under-recognised. We aimed to estimate the prevalence in an asymptomatic population and to identify demographic and clinical predictors using the UK Biobank data. Materials and methods DXA spine images from 2446 asymptomatic UK Biobank participants aged 40–79 years were analysed retrospectively. Vertebral fractures were defined as moderate or severe deformities (≥ 25% vertebral height loss). Fractures were identified using an artificial-intelligence-assisted six-point morphometric algorithm with manual correction and radiologist confirmation. Associations with age, sex, bone mineral density (BMD), body mass index (BMI), medication, and back pain were analysed. Results A total of 2446 participants (mean age 62.0 ± 7.4 years; 1151 men) were analysed. Moderate or severe vertebral fractures were identified in 356 participants (14.6%). Prevalence increased with age, from 9.4% in participants aged 40–49 years to 19.6% in those aged 70–79 years. Fractures were more common in men than women (18.8% vs. 10.8%; adjusted OR 0.51 for women vs. men, 95% CI 0.40–0.66; p < 0.001). BMD and most conventional clinical risk factors had limited predictive value. Conclusions Silent vertebral fractures are common in midlife, frequently occur in individuals with normal bone density, and are more prevalent in men. Conventional clinical risk factors have a limited ability to identify affected individuals. Key Points Question Silent vertebral fractures are frequently overlooked in asymptomatic individuals, and their prevalence and demographic distribution in middle-aged adults are not well-characterised . Findings In a large asymptomatic cohort, vertebral fractures were common, showed male predominance, and were frequently present in individuals without low bone mineral density or recognised clinical risk factors . Clinical relevance Silent vertebral fractures are prevalent in asymptomatic adults and are poorly captured by conventional risk assessment, indicating limitations of current approaches to fracture identification .

This study examines the impact of integrating artificial intelligence tools on the principle of good administration, enshrined in Article 41 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union, focusing on the guarantee of a reasonable time for resolving administrative requests. The paper begins with the legal and case-law foundation of the reasonable time standard, both at European level (ECtHR and CJEU case law) and at national level (Romanian court practice and the express regulation of time limits in Romanian legislation), before analysing, in a second stage, the positive contributions that digitalisation may bring to compliance with this standard: faster processing of standardised requests, reduction of human error, increased transparency and accountability, easier access to public information, and optimisation of complex procedures. The study also identifies the structural limits of this positive impact and the autonomous risks generated by the use of AI – technological dependency, algorithmic errors, excessive standardisation, algorithmic opacity, diluted accountability and unequal access to performant digital resources. The central conclusion is that, in the age of artificial intelligence, the reasonable time standard becomes a dynamic standard, whose observance depends on a set of institutional and technological safeguards.

Abstract—The cross-organizational sharing of high-dimensional empirical datasets—such as electronic health records, financial credit transactions, and telecommunications telemetry—is fundamentally constrained by strict data governance legislation (e.g., GDPR, HIPAA, CCPA). Heuristic sanitization methods (such as k-anonymity, l-diversity, and pseudo-anonymization) have repeatedly proven vulnerable to linkage and re-identification attacks. Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI)—encompassing Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs), Variational Autoencoders (VAEs), and Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models (DDPMs)—offers the capability to synthesize structurally authentic surrogate populations. However, unconstrained generative models memorize sensitive training instances within their parameter weights, exposing downstream deployments to Membership Inference Attacks (MIA) and Attribute Disclosure Attacks. Differential Privacy (DP) provides the mathematical standard to guarantee bounded information leakage independent of adversarial prior knowledge. This paper presents an exhaustive, mathematically formal technical investigation and empirical benchmark of Privacy-Preserving Synthetic Data Generation uniting Generative AI with Differential Privacy. We formalize the Renyi Differential Privacy (RDP) accounting framework, model gradient perturbation dynamics under Differentially Private Stochastic Gradient Descent (DP-SGD), and evaluate discrete marginal mechanisms (PrivBayes, PGM) alongside continuous generative models (DP-WGAN, DP-Diffusion). Furthermore, we construct an enterprise benchmarking testbed across three high-dimensional, sensitive datasets (MIMIC-III clinical records, German Credit, and Census PUMS). Our findings demonstrate that while unconstrained generative synthesis suffers a 74.2% membership inference vulnerability, DP-Diffusion governed by (epsilon = 1.0, delta = 10^-5) bounds attacker advantage to near-random guessing (51.8%) while preserving 91.4% downstream machine learning classification utility. Finally, we formulate open challenges in high-dimensional privacy budgeting, multi-modal alignment, and verified auditing frameworks. Index Terms—Differential Privacy (DP), Generative AI, Synthetic Data Generation, DP-SGD, Diffusion Models, Membership Inference Attacks (MIA), Renyi Differential Privacy, Data Governance.

Abstract This article looks at the deregulation of US prison labor in the 1970s and 1980s, and the use of prison labor in information technology (IT) and digital electronics supply chains. The article, on one hand, locates the effort to deregulate prison labor in US electronics firms’ search for cheap labor enclaves and the uneven development of the postwar United States. At the same time, the article situiates this deregulatory turn in the progressive reforms of the 1970s. These reforms, which occurred first at the state and local levels, sought to promote prisoner welfare, provide opportunities for “self-help,” and rationalize the allocation of state and local resources in light of rising inflation. As such, the article complicates narratives of the rise of neoliberalism, which center issues like “lost confidence” in the efficacy of federal social welfare programs, breaches in public trust following Watergate, the 1973 oil shock, knock-on effects of New Deal and Great Society programs, or emerging “family values” and racist dog-whistle politics. It also frames the labor history of digital electronics in a way that supports an analysis of the relationship between capitalist development and US federalism aongside the particularities of firm-level motivation, insitutional inertia, and prevailing political ideology. Current discussions of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and corrections largely focus on the use of incarcerated persons to train AI algorithms or the use of AI systems to surveil prisoners. However, this article centers the growth of tech supply chains in the 1970s and 1980s as an important precursor to the development of contemporary AI technology and firms.

Abstract LLM agents increasingly call tools and take irreversible actions, yet the reasoning that licenses an action is rarely checked before execution. We present Proof-Carrying Agent Actions (PCAA) : each governed action carries a typed Action Certificate that a planner-independent checker must accept before execution. A trusted execution shim derives the obligation set and the irreversibility classification from an authoritative tool contract and binds the certificate to the exact invocation with a canonical SHA-256 commitment. The checker compares that context with the certificate, re-derives typed support (proof, belief, hypothesis, contingency, conflict, or no-progress), and validates formula-level inference rules. Irreversible actions require Proof for every declared licensing obligation. The checker accepts the two valid certificates and rejects all fifteen unsafe certificates in a semantic battery; four additional structural cases confirm rejection of argument substitution, precondition omission, and risk-flag downgrade. A microbenchmark of a three-obligation payment certificate measures 53.7 μs median and 65.7 μs p95 for construction, checking, serialization, and buffered local persistence. A stateful guardrail with the same certified-state predicate matches PCAA on safety; PCAA’s distinct contribution is a typed, replayable decision artifact. Guarantees are relative to trusted tool contracts: PCAA checks their use, not their real-world semantic correctness.

This study examined public affairs communication in the era of climate change and artificial intelligence: strategies for policy and advocacy and governance in Nigeria. The technological determinism theory was anchored in this study. This study adopted a qualitative research method, utilising in-depth interviews to explore the role of artificial intelligence in public affairs communication for climate policy advocacy and governance in Nigeria. The population of the study consisted of 120 key stakeholders involved in climate policy advocacy and governance, including government officials, policymakers, environmental NGOs, media professionals and AI experts. The sample size comprised 20 purposively selected respondents with expertise in climate policy, artificial intelligence applications in governance and public affairs communication. The sampling technique used was purposive sampling, allowing the selection of individuals who possess specialized knowledge and experience relevant to the study. The method of data collection involves semi-structured, in-depth interviews and method of data analysis followed thematic analysis, where transcribed interview data were systematically coded to identify emerging patterns, themes and relationships. The findings revealed that, AI-driven tools significantly enhance public affairs communication by improving message dissemination, audience targeting and engagement strategies in climate advocacy. AI-powered chatbots, predictive analytics and automated content generation have been instrumental in personalizing climate messages and countering misinformation. The study concluded that AI has emerged as a transformative tool in public affairs communication, enabling more effective climate advocacy through targeted messaging, audience engagement and misinformation management. However, its full potential can only be realised if challenges such as algorithmic bias, inadequate digital infrastructure and the need for human-centred communication strategies are addressed. The study recommended that Policymakers and communication professionals should invest in AIdriven tools while ensuring ethical guidelines and human-centred approaches to enhance climate advocacy in Nigeria

Abstract The emergence of large language models (LLMs) has fundamentally transformed information interaction, yet their application in environmental science and engineering (ESE) is hindered by multimodal data formats, dynamic context requirements, and hallucination risks. To transition from general-purpose models to domain expert agentic systems, this Perspective introduces a three-pillar framework for ESE-LLMs: domain perception, knowledge grounding, and action capability. Implementing these capabilities introduces potential pitfalls such as geographic representation bias, catastrophic forgetting, and source authenticity vulnerabilities, which require strategic model blending and careful data curation to overcome. Furthermore, rigorous evaluation must extend beyond standard knowledge benchmarks to systematically assess factuality, fairness, consistency, and safety using both human and automated metrics. Finally, we present a decision-guided deployment workflow that helps researchers in ESE fields integrate LLMs into their workflow. Ultimately, achieving trustworthy environmental intelligence relies on continuous evaluation, robust governance, and sustained interdisciplinary collaboration to safely deploy agentic ESE-LLMs for high-stakes environmental challenges.

documents.abstract: Quantum Sociodynamics (QSD) is introduced as a computational method for modelling symbolic influence and trust in artificial-intelligence-supported sustainable city transitions. Its central object, the Symbolic Mediation Field, represents how actor orientations, source–audience relations and communication histories shape signal effects. Actor states are encoded by complex variables ψi, symbolic transport by U(1) link variables Uij, signed coupling by qi and external interventions by Ji. Gauge-invariant measures capture local alignment, path transport and loop holonomy. Formal analysis establishes invariance under local re-description, path independence under zero holonomy and a classical DeGroot–Friedkin–Johnsen limit. Deterministic simulations demonstrate response reversal, order effects and persistent relational change after institutional shocks. A 27-record heat-pump corpus illustrates application to AI-assisted urban decarbonisation governance and identifies validation requirements.

The post-pandemic labor landscape has witnessed the rise of "quiet quitting"—a behavioral phenomenon where employees strictly adhere to their contractual job descriptions while withholding discretionary extra-role behaviors, discretionary effort, and voluntary over-time involvement. While often framed by mainstream media as an expression of worker apathy, this study conceptualizes quiet quitting as a structural symptom of workplace burnout, organizational injustice, and systemic psychological contract breach. Through a comprehensive evaluation using Conservation of Resources (COR) theory, Social Exchange Theory (SET), and the Job Demands-Resources (JD-R) model, this paper examines the cascading operational, psychological, and financial impacts of quiet quitting on long-term organizational sustainability. I argue that relying on short-term extra-role extraction undermines triple-bottom-line organizational health. Ultimately, quiet quitting is not an expression of employee indolence, but a strategic self-preservation mechanism in response to prolonged work stress, unmet organizational expectations, and systemic burnout. Finally, an evidence-based strategic framework is offered to realign managerial practices, work-design architectures, and performance metrics to foster sustainable workforce resilience as well as recommendations are posited.

This study proposes an uncertainty-aware collision-risk evaluation framework for the safe navigation of autonomous ships. Target-ship information obtained from the Automatic Identification System (AIS) and radar is characterized by discrete update intervals and measurement uncertainty, which can degrade situational awareness and collision-avoidance decision-making. To address this problem, an Unscented Kalman Filter (UKF) was used to fuse AIS and radar data and estimate target-ship states and associated uncertainties in real time. The resulting state-estimation covariance was incorporated into the Quaternion Ship Domain (QSD) to construct a probabilistic ship domain that reflects target-position uncertainty. Based on this domain, Probabilistic Collision Exposure (PCE) was defined as a velocity-space collision-exposure metric representing the proportion of collision-causing velocity vectors within the own ship's reachable velocity set, while Expected Collision Energy (ECE) was formulated to incorporate the potential collision consequence. The framework was evaluated through MMG-based simulations involving head-on, starboard crossing, nonlinear maneuvering, and three-target multiple-encounter scenarios under delayed and noisy sensing conditions. In the nonlinear maneuvering scenario, the target-position error remained within approximately 5 m, with an average error of approximately 3 m. Compared with the conventional Collision Risk Index (CRI), PCE showed substantially lower residual risk after the closest point of approach (CPA) in the representative head-on and starboard crossing scenarios. The post-CPA residual area-under-the-curve (AUC) ratios were 2.21% and 0.59% for PCE in the head-on and starboard crossing scenarios, respectively, compared with 32.80% and 40.48% for CRI. The three-target scenario further demonstrated target-specific collision-exposure evaluation and simultaneous multi-target avoidance, while the implemented framework maintained its nominal 10-Hz system update cycle across the evaluated single-target and multi-target simulations.

When a clinical AI system’s output differs from a human clinician’s judgment, what follows is consequential and underspecified. Current AI interfaces offer only a narrow lane for what happens next: they present the AI output (and its associated potential divergence) as an adjudicative choice for a human to accept, override, or modify. In practice, collapsing this human-AI interaction into a single output inadvertently obscures what happens in a potential divergence event (Fig. 1 ) which can be characterized along three axes: What the workflow and interface allow the clinician to see and do ( structural axis), what information each side brought to the interaction ( informational axis), and how the clinician engaged with the AI’s reasoning rather than only its output ( behavioral axis). When clinical judgment and AI output diverge, clinicians must ultimately decide what to recommend and how to explain their recommendation to the patient, consider their autonomy, accountability, and liability, and bear moral responsibility 1 . A recent systematic review of AI ethics in nursing and midwifery found that AI challenges the role of health professionals not through replacement, but through subtle reconfiguration of the activities that count as care and that emphasis on AI efficiency may risk certain relational aspects of care less visible and valued 2 . Because clinicians often cannot see how an AI system reached its output, they are left to choose between that AI output and their own judgment. Clinicians are told to be the “human in the loop” but are typically given no method for doing so beyond “exercising their judgment” 3 . Efforts to make AI output both more technically explainable and human interpretable - have not directly correlated with improved clinical decisions and have sometimes created false confidence in incorrect AI output 4 .

documents.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) and large language models (LLMs) are transforming clinical decision support systems (CDSS) from traditional discrete predictions into fluent, context-aware clinical narrative generation. Although these capabilities substantially improve the efficiency of clinical workflows, they also introduce distinctive cognitive challenges: highly fluent and seemingly plausible medical narratives may reshape the way physicians construct clinical meaning and make analytic judgments. This perspective paper introduces the concept of Narrative Cognitive Substitution (NCS), proposed as a testable mid-level theoretical construct, which describes the hypothesized shift in human cognition from active hypothesis generation to passive retrospective validation when GenAI outputs pre-organize diagnostic reasoning and therapeutic pathways. We further propose a Skill Evolution Framework that characterizes the potential effects of GenAI on physician competence across five trajectories: Augmentation, Restructuring, Deskilling, Never-skilling, and Mis-skilling. In addition, we analyze the resulting Accountability Gap: although algorithmic outputs are increasingly embedded in clinical decision-making, decision influence is distributed across clinicians, institutions, developers, and deployers, yet professional accountability and final decision authority remain formally concentrated on the individual physician. To address these systemic challenges, we propose a human-centered governance framework —presented as design hypotheses requiring prospective evaluation— encompassing user interface design (embedding risk-adaptive cognitive friction), medical education (establishing targeted, protected AI-free reasoning exercises (“Reasoning Cleanrooms”)), and institutional policies (implementing substantive human oversight and algorithmovigilance). We argue that the goal of digital health governance should not be to maximize automation, but rather to safeguard human cognitive agency, diagnostic vigilance, and layered, distributed accountability within AI-enabled healthcare systems.

documents.abstract: To distinguish between “text improvement” and “cognitive gain” in generative-AI-assisted second language learning, this study proposes a Multimodal Intervention-Aware Temporal Graph Network (MITG-Net). The method integrates human-AI dialogue, revision trajectories, behavioral logs, and learner attributes. Through intervention-conditioned dynamic weighting and heterogeneous temporal graph modeling, it captures the relationships among prompts, feedback, revisions, and transfer, and jointly performs intervention-effect recognition and learning-behavior-pattern discovery. Experiments were conducted on 744 learning sessions collected from 186 undergraduates at three universities. MITG-Net achieved a Macro-F1 of 0.816 and a weighted Kappa of 0.854, outperforming the strongest baseline, HGT, by 3.4 percentage points in Macro-F1. Removing behavioral logs and revision trajectories reduced Macro-F1 by 0.054 and 0.045, respectively. The model identified five behavior patterns. Among them, the strategy-transfer application pattern achieved an average effect level of 2.78 and a transfer score of 0.82, substantially higher than the 1.36 and 0.31 obtained by the AI-dominated direct-adoption pattern. These results demonstrate that the proposed method can effectively recognize cognitive intervention effects and provide interpretable evidence for personalized support in second language learning.

documents.abstract: The development of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) has transformed the learning ecology by positioning AI as a cognitive partner that supports personalisation, feedback, problem-solving, and creativity. This transformation necessitates a reconstruction of the concept of self-actualisation, as some human cognitive activities can be delegated to AI. This study aims to analyse the transformation of self actualisation, identify the conditions that strengthen or hinder it, and formulate a conceptual framework for self-actualisation in AI-based learning. This study employs a qualitative library research approach using an integrative literature review design. The findings indicate that GenAI is paradoxical in nature: it can serve as a cognitive scaffold that strengthens autonomy, competence, self-regulation, creativity, metacognition, and epistemic agency, while also potentially encouraging cognitive offloading, dependence, and the weakening of cognitive autonomy. This study proposes the Reflective-Relational Self Actualisation Framework in AI Learning Ecologies (RRSA-AILE), which encompasses autonomy, competence, relatedness, epistemic agency, metacognitive reflexivity, generative creativity, and ethical responsibility. Theoretically, RRSA-AILE integrates humanism, Self-Determination Theory, Self-Regulated Learning, and learner agency. Practically, the framework provides a foundation for AI-enhanced learning that is augmentative, reflective, and centred on human agency.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence is transforming the knowledge structure of medicine and reshaping how physicians are trained across undergraduate medical education, residency, and continuing professional development. As predictive algorithms increasingly perform pattern recognition tasks once central to clinical expertise, the definition of “core medical knowledge” is shifting toward data literacy, probabilistic reasoning, interdisciplinary collaboration, and ethical oversight of intelligent systems. This chapter examines how AI-assisted and AI-integrated learning environments are altering the roles of memorization, diagnostic reasoning, and clinical decision making, while creating new expectations for physicians as interpreters of algorithmic outputs rather than sole generators of diagnostic insight. It explores emerging educational models incorporating simulation, adaptive tutoring systems, multimodal decision support tools, and lifelong learning infrastructures embedded within digital health systems. Ultimately, reimagining medical education requires balancing technological capability with human judgment so that clinicians remain central to safe, equitable, and patient-centered care in an increasingly automated healthcare environment.

documents.abstract: Abstract Objective To characterise the reporting completeness of clinical trials involving large language model (LLM) interventions using established reporting guidelines. Design Systematic review and meta-research analysis. Data sources Bibliographic databases (Embase, Medline, and CENTRAL) were searched for trial reports and protocols, and trial registries (ClinicalTrials.gov and World Health Organization International Clinical Trials Registry Platform) were searched for trial registrations published from 1 January 2017 to 6 December 2025. Eligibility criteria Trial reports, trial protocols, and trial registrations describing clinical trials of LLM interventions in medicine. LLM interventions used for a healthcare function in a clinical trial setting included patient education, clinical documentation, communication support, triage, care navigation, management recommendations, or clinical decision support. Eligible studies prospectively assigned human participants to the intervention and evaluated a health related biomedical or behavioural outcome. Main outcome measures Overall study level and item level reporting completeness assessed using reporting guidelines matched to study design and purpose, including TRIPOD-LLM (Transparent Reporting of a multivariable prediction model for Individual Prognosis Or Diagnosis—LLM), CONSORT (Consolidated Standards of Reporting Trials) 2025 and CONSORT-AI, SPIRIT (Standard Protocol Items: Recommendations for Interventional Trials) 2025 and SPIRIT-AI, CHART (Chatbot Assessment Reporting Tool), and the WHO Trial Registration Dataset (version 1.3.1). Two reviewers independently screened and extracted trial and intervention characteristics, and three calibrated raters assessed item level reporting completeness. Results The systematic search yielded 461 records, including 68 trial reports, 15 protocols, and 378 registrations. Trial reports were predominantly small sample, single site randomised studies published between 2024 and 2025, spanning diverse clinical specialties and primarily targeting patient facing education and management recommendations. Mean reporting completeness was modest across eligible trial reports (TRIPOD-LLM 40%, CONSORT 2025 44%, CONSORT-AI 59%, CHART 52%), trial protocols (SPIRIT 2025 51%, SPIRIT-AI 57%), and trial registrations (WHO Trial Registration Dataset 61%). Clinical trial reports of LLM interventions prioritise narrative framing and commentary over the methodological detail needed for replication, risk-of-bias assessment, and governance of model performance over time. Critical methodological elements for reproducibility, including data and intervention provenance, input preprocessing, model versioning and access modality, inference parameters, output postprocessing, as well as protocol, data, and code access, were inconsistently reported. Harms planning, monitoring, and reporting were often incompletely reported, limiting the critical appraisal of the safety of LLM interventions in healthcare. Conclusion Clinical trials of LLM interventions show modest adherence to established reporting guidelines, with persistent underreporting of LLM specific methodological details, reproducibility artefacts (protocols, data, code), and harms reporting required to support reproducibility and confident appraisal of safety risks before their clinical translation.

documents.abstract: This article reconstructs a history of language, reason, and practical activity from Augustine through Kant, Hegel, Marx, the European linguistic turn, and analytic philosophy in order to formulate the concept of reproductive iden tity. Reproductive identity is not sameness, a fixed inner essence, or the final conceptual possession of the world. It is the historically open, materially conditioned work through which embodied individuals and communities sustain, repair, and develop the relations that enable their continuation. Augustine’s psychological trinity supplies an early grammar of memory, understanding, and will or love; Kant clarifies the conditions of judgment and practical reason; Hegel understands concept and reality as mutually realised in activity; and Marx translates this movement into the communal metabolism through which human beings reproduce life in and through nature. The linguistic turn and an alytic philosophy provide indispensable accounts of disclosure, difference, reference, truth, use, and normativity. The section on analytic philosophy distinguishes formal validity from situated inquiry and reconstructs practical reason as both normatively articulated and causally efficacious. Neither tradition, however, can settle the material and in stitutional conditions of the forms of life in which language works. The final sections develop ecological democracy and politically subordinate artificial intelligence as institutional consequences of the argument. Artificial intelligence is treated not as a sovereign subject but as a reversible public infrastructure whose legitimacy depends on ecological admissibility, traceability, contestability, repair, and the common reproduction of internal and external nature.

Abstract Despite growing clinical adoption of artificial intelligence in radiology, fewer than one in five commercially available models are cleared for paediatric use. Existing systems are trained predominantly on adult data and generalize poorly to neonates, yet efficient strategies for repurposing them without data sharing or large-scale local data curation are lacking. Here we present an international retrospective study of neonatal chest radiographs from 30 neonatal intensive care units across 20 countries and territories, evaluating continual learning as a privacy-preserving approach to adapt a deep learning model for adult endotracheal tube assessment to neonatal care. Each hospital contributed 50 radiographs for sequential model retraining without centralized data pooling. Continual learning achieved lower anatomical landmark localization error (0.67 cm versus 1.29 cm for hospital-specific fine-tuning and 4.30 cm for adult-only models) at 29 of 30 sites, with improved detection of deep intubations at 27 of 30 sites. These findings demonstrate that privacy-preserving collaborative learning can address critical gaps in paediatric AI deployment.

documents.abstract: Rapid situational awareness is a cornerstone of effective civil protection and disaster response, demanding highly resilient localization and decision-support capabilities under challenging environmental conditions. This paper presents RESCUE-AR (Responsive Sensor-Fusion for Civil-Protection and Disaster Response Using Mobile Augmented Reality), a conceptual and methodological framework for mobile Augmented Reality (AR) systems designed to support emergency operations through heterogeneous and adaptive sensor fusion. This work formalizes the mathematical and algorithmic architecture of the RESCUE-AR framework, establishing an adaptive multi-sensor measurement fusion strategy, integrating Visual SLAM, IMU, depth sensing, and GNSS data to enhance robustness in environments affected by occlusion, signal degradation, and dynamic change. The framework is grounded in a systematic literature review that identifies the limitations of single-sensor and fixed-weight fusion approaches in disaster scenarios and motivates the adoption of adaptive fusion strategies. An initial user-centered evaluation is conducted through a structured approach, employing standardized questionnaires to assess usability, cognitive workload, anticipated operational trust, and framework suitability for first responders. The results indicate strong perceived utility, reduced cognitive load, and high confidence in AR-assisted decision-making, supporting the potential of adaptive sensor-fusion-based mobile AR as a viable and scalable decision-support tool for civil protection and disaster response.

Background/Objectives: This study utilizes machine learning (ML) models integrated with explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) to perform a retrospective analysis of factors associated with tuberculosis (TB) treatment duration and outcomes. Methods: Two datasets comprising completed TB patient records from a Malaysian hospital were analyzed. Significant features were identified using Pearson correlation for treatment duration and the Boruta algorithm for treatment outcome. Support Vector Regressor (SVR) was used to evaluate treatment duration, while Logistic Regression, Random Forest, and XGBoost were evaluated for treatment outcome classification. SHapley Additive Explanations (SHAP) was integrated to enhance model interpretability. Results: On the primary dataset (Dataset A), SVRPearson demonstrated the best performance for treatment duration (MAE = 44.18 days, R2 = 0.54), although performance decreased on the external dataset (Dataset B: MAE = 71.33 days, R2 = 0.11), partly due to missing feature imputations. For treatment outcome classification, XGBoostBoruta achieved an accuracy of 99.20% on Dataset A and 97.34% on Dataset B. SHAP feature attribution indicated that treatment outcome was the primary contributor to treatment duration, whereas treatment status and treatment duration were the dominant features contributing to the treatment outcome model. Conclusions: These findings demonstrate the value of explainable machine learning for characterizing factors associated with TB treatment duration and outcomes in completed treatment episodes and supporting retrospective clinical audit and post hoc case interpretation.

The global prevalence of chronic diseases is becoming increasingly severe, and traditional care models are confronted with multiple challenges, including uneven distribution of medical resources, insufficient continuity of care, and inadequate patient self-management capacity. The rapid iteration of digital technologies and the catalyst of the COVID-19 pandemic have driven chronic disease care into a new phase of digital transformation. Based on relevant studies published from 2021 to 2026, this paper structures its analysis around a core logical framework: evidence-based evidence, care models, population adaptability and practical implementation. It systematically reviews the core technical systems and innovative characteristics of care models in digital chronic disease care, deeply analyzes the adaptive differences across diverse populations and disease types, and conducts critical reflections from the perspectives of evidence quality, health equity, clinical applicability, and homogeneity in intervention design. Finally, it puts forward future development directions centered on precision, localization, equity, and integration. The study reveals that digital chronic disease care has formed four core technological systems in application: intelligent sensing, digital behavioral intervention, immersive technology, and artificial intelligence (AI) and big data. Care models demonstrate innovative trends of nurse leadership, multi-dimensional collaboration, and caregiver empowerment. Nevertheless, prominent issues persist, such as insufficient high-quality evidence, a striking digital divide, difficulties in clinical integration, and a lack of personalized design. In the future, deep integration of technological innovation with clinical demands, enhanced targeted interventions for vulnerable populations, implementation of localized long-term studies, and improvement of policy and ethical guarantee systems are required. These efforts will promote the shift of digital chronic disease care from technology-driven to evidence-driven and demand-driven models, ultimately improving the overall efficiency of chronic disease management and health equity.

A fundamental limitation of current predictive maintenance is the inability to transform prognostic uncertainty into actionable decisions, which often leads to either wasteful early interventions or catastrophic failures in aero-engines. To address this, we propose the Risk-Aware Predictive Maintenance (RAPM) framework consisting of four integrated components: a probabilistic stacked sparse autoencoder that extracts degradation features while providing distributional remaining useful life (RUL) predictions; a Monte Carlo Dropout module with Conditional Value at Risk (CVaR) that summarizes lower-tail predictive risk and produces a conservative RUL estimate for decision making; a locally deployed large language model (Qwen2.5-3B) that abstracts numerical uncertainty into discrete semantic risk levels, enabling interpretable reward shaping; and a Proximal Policy Optimization agent trained with curriculum learning to handle long-horizon sparse-reward maintenance optimization. On the NASA C-MAPSS FD001 benchmark, RAPM achieves a 96.0% optimal stopping rate with no late interventions or failure events compared with 90.2% for the strongest independent maintenance baseline. Under controlled substitution with LSTM-MCD, Transformer-MCD, CNN-MCD, and Deep Ensemble prognostic backbones, the same CVaR-LLM-PPO decision architecture maintains optimal stopping rates of 92.4–95.2% with no late interventions or failure events. Within the matched Rule-PPO ablation, CVaR increases the mean optimal stopping rate from 92.0% to 95.0% under unperturbed conditions, which is a gain of 3.0 percentage points. Under Gaussian sensor noise (σ=0.05), the gain reaches 9.0 percentage points, from 73.0% to 82.0%. These results demonstrate that the decision benefit of RAPM extends across independently trained prognostic models.

Abstract - The convergence of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and biotechnology is revolutionizing scientific research, healthcare, and industrial applications. This paper examines how AI techniques, like computer vision, machine learning, deep learning, and NLP, are revolutionizing important biotechnology fields like drug discovery, genomics, personalized medicine, agricultural innovation, and industrial bioprocessing. AI enables faster data analysis, accurate prediction of biological behaviors, and automation of complex tasks, significantly accelerating the pace of innovation. We also discuss commonly used AI tools in biotechnology and highlight the growth of AI-driven biotech startups. The incorporation of AI presents a number of obstacles despite its transformative potential, such as the requirement for transparent algorithms, ethical issues, and data privacy concerns. The goal of the article is to provide a thorough review of the state of affairs, recent developments, and potential future progress in the nexus of biotechnology and artificial intelligence.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence is increasingly embedded in clinical decision making, raising complex questions about safety, accountability, and regulatory oversight when algorithmic recommendations contribute to harm. Unlike traditional medical devices, many AI systems evolve over time, operate across institutional boundaries, and depend on dynamic datasets, making responsibility for errors distributed among clinicians, developers, and healthcare organizations. This chapter examines emerging regulatory frameworks governing clinical AI, including validation standards, post-market surveillance requirements, and lifecycle oversight approaches developed by agencies such as the U.S. Food and Drug Administration and international regulators. It also explores how clinicians can evaluate predictive models before adoption by assessing transparency, calibration, fairness, and generalizability. Understanding shared accountability in AI-assisted care is essential to ensuring safe implementation without slowing innovation. Ultimately, effective governance will depend on collaboration among clinicians, engineers, institutions, and regulators to create trustworthy systems that improve outcomes while protecting patients.

documents.abstract: This research paper investigates the severe educational resource scarcity in Balochistan, and its impact on student learning outcomes and career Preparation. Regardless of growing youth populations, public and private educational institutions in the region face widespread systemic challenges. Based on survey data his study shows how local education falls short in basic school facilities, modern technology subjects, practical career training, global exam access, college degree tracks, and extracurricular activities. Specifically, over 69% of local students rely on government schools plagued by broken facilities, missing basic utilities, and unmonitored teacher absenteeism. Furthermore, institutions suffer from a complete absence of modern fields like Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Robotics, poor quality in practical computer-based training, extreme financial barriers in advanced schooling (A-Levels), a total lack of international test centers (SAT/TOEFL), and a major shortage of sports, public speaking, and student development programs. The paper also highlights severe gender disparities caused by unsafe transport options and domestic burdens. To bridge the gap between classroom instruction and modern market requirements, this study proposes key policy recommendations, including targeted infrastructure investment, institutional accountability, curriculum modernization, fully equipped science and computer laboratories, structured career counseling, extracurricular programs (sports and Model United Nations), and safe, dedicated transportation for female students.

Scientific reasoning moves beyond natural language. The search for a discovery runs across sequences, structures, fields, omics, images and measurements, while language models reason mainly in text. This Perspective sets out four proposals from the Scinetics team. First, we define science tokens: modality-appropriate units of scientific information, spanning native discrete symbols, typed values, continuous representations and learned, decodable codes. A shared interface for these representations would let one model read, write and reason across modalities, so that a chain of science tokens operates on scientifically meaningful states, not on descriptions of them. Second, we define Scientific Super Intelligence (SSI) as a joint crossover: one frozen model that outperforms vertical specialists, such as the AlphaFold series on protein structure prediction, on their own tasks, and outperforms general large language models of the same size on broad scientific reasoning. Capacity, published training precedents, data inventories and compute place the first test of that crossover at 100–300 billion parameters and 10–30 trillion training tokens. Third, we propose ScienceRSI (Science Recursive Self- Improvement) as the route to that window. Following the AI4AI pattern, each larger generation is trained on data that the smaller generation before it produced: the earlier model generates candidate reasoning, screens it and keeps what passes, and in science that screening can be done by a simulation, a database or an experiment. Training this way reduces the dependence on scarce human-written scientific reasoning data and shortens each iteration. Fourth, we propose science-token economics, which separates metered computation from the value of evidence-labelled, reusable scientific assets.

The author presents newly derived differential constitutive relations (equations) of the second fractional order for complex, higher-level rheological models of fractional-type viscoelastic materials with piezoelectric properties. These newly derived differential equations are of the second fractional order and incorporate Caputo differential operators of the first and second fractional orders. The lecturer outlines an approximate analytical methodology for solving these second-fractional-order differential equations, employing the Laplace transform, expansion into power series with respect to the complex Laplace parameter, and the properties of the convolution of three functions. This methodology yields approximate analytical solutions for the mew derived second-fractional-order differential constitutive equations governing these complex, higher-level rheological materials. These approximate analytical solutions simultaneously serve as integral constitutive relations, establishing the link between normal stresses and axial strains in these complex, higher-level rheological models of fractional-type viscoelastic materials with piezoelectric properties. The theoretical analytical results obtained pertain to complex fractional-type material models, specifically the second-level complexity Letherish-Faraday model for a fractional-type viscoelastic material with piezoelectric properties; The Jeffreys-Faraday model represents a second-level complexity rheological model for a fractional-type viscoelastic material with piezoelectric properties, while the Burgers-Faraday model represents a third-level complexity model of the same type. These three rheological models of higher complexity—in their classical linear forms—are already widely used; the author believes that the newly introduced fractional-type models (named by the author) will also see widespread application, initially in the validation of experimental research and subsequently in practical use. The lecturer also believes that these results open up new challenges regarding the development of software for calculating inverse Laplace transforms of complex Laplace-transformed expressions, thereby expanding the scope of artificial intelligence in areas where it is currently underdeveloped and limited.

This research explores secondary education teachers" perceptions regarding the integration of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) into instructional practice. Through semi-structured interviews with a sample of ten (10) educators from diverse academic backgrounds, the study examines three core pillars: interaction and usability, issues of trust and ethics, and the transformation of professional identity. The findings reveal that using AI tools is a complex cognitive process requiring strategic prompt engineering. Despite the small sample size, participants consistently demonstrated a "cautious acceptance," acting as critical evaluators of machine-generated outputs to mitigate scientific inaccuracies and "hallucinations." In conclusion, the study highlights a shift in the teaching role from being a source of knowledge to an authority of critical mediation. It emphasizes the urgent need for professional development that fosters pedagogical agency and ethical action within the modern digital learning environment.

documents.abstract: Abstract—As cellular architectures transition from 5G toward Sixth-Generation (6G) wireless networks, the classical Shannon-Nyquist paradigm of bit-level data transmission is rapidly approaching its theoretical physical channel capacity limits. Ultra-dense Internet of Things (IoT) ecosystems, autonomous vehicular swarms, and extended reality (XR) telepresence demand terabit-per-second (Tbps) data rates, sub-millisecond latencies, and continuous real-time edge artificial intelligence (AI) inference over severely bandwidth-constrained wireless channels. Classical communications optimize bit error rates (BER), transmitting massive streams of uncompressed binary representations regardless of the underlying computational task. Semantic Communications and Task-Oriented Edge Intelligence establish a transformative paradigm shift: shifting the transmission objective from error-free bit reconstruction to the faithful transmission of actionable semantic meaning and task-relevant latent features. By uniting Deep Joint Source-Channel Coding (Deep JSCC) with transformer-based feature extractors, semantic communication frameworks filter out redundant sensory data at the transmitter, communicating only task-critical representations to edge compute nodes. However, deploying semantic communications over stochastic wireless channels introduces acute foundational challenges: semantic noise induced by channel fading, joint training instability across non-differentiable wireless channels, and catastrophic performance degradation under out-of-distribution physical channel shifts. This paper presents an exhaustive, mathematically formal technical investigation and empirical benchmark of semantic communications for 6G edge intelligence. We formalize the rate-distortion-perception tradeoff under Weaver-Shannon semantic communication tiers, model continuous-time Deep JSCC over Rayleigh and Rician fading channels, and establish Lyapunov-guided end-to-end latency bounds for distributed edge inference. Furthermore, we construct an empirical software-defined radio (SDR) and GPU testbed evaluating multimodal perception and edge autonomous vehicle telemetry under severe signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) degradation. Our empirical findings demonstrate that Deep JSCC semantic transmission achieves a 78.4% reduction in required channel bandwidth while preserving 94.6% downstream edge classification accuracy under extreme channel noise (SNR = -6 dB), where classical JPEG/264 paired with LDPC coding completely collapses. Finally, we formulate open research directions in semantic knowledge base synchronization, neuro-symbolic semantic verification, and zero-trust semantic cybersecurity. Index Terms—Semantic Communications, 6G Wireless Networks, Edge Intelligence, Deep Joint Source-Channel Coding (Deep JSCC), Task-Oriented Communications, Shannon-Weaver Levels, Physical Layer AI.

Abstract Prior research has shown that customers’ perceptions of chatbots may be influenced by the situational context in which human–chatbot interactions take place. This research advances understanding of artificial intelligence (AI)‐enabled chatbot‐led service failure recovery (SFR) in the context of customer loyalty. Using a social constructivist philosophical perspective and an inductive approach, 52 in‐depth interviews were conducted to capture individuals’ perceptions of chatbot‐led interactions during a SFR process and how these perceptions impacted their trust in, and commitment to, brands. Utilizing commitment‐trust theory and trust transfer theory, we propose a framework that characterizes the relationships between a chatbot‐led SFR process and customer loyalty intentions. Based on the emergent data, customers’ evaluations of a service recovery journey led by chatbots can be grouped into four main outcomes: continued trust in, and commitment to, chatbot and brand; continued trust in, and commitment to, brand; discontinued trust in, and commitment to, chatbot; and discontinued trust in, and commitment to, chatbot and brand. Our findings extend current understanding of how consumers’ trust and commitment during chatbot‐led interactions during SFR evolve and highlight the dynamic relationship between consumers and the context of interactions. This study has theoretical and practical implications for developing and leveraging customers’ loyalty in AI‐enabled chatbot‐led SFR environments.

This article examines sharenting practices among parents in relation to the recognition of the child's agency and the underlying relational mechanisms, interpreted through the lens of Educational Transactional Analysis (ETA). The empirical study employed a questionnaire-based survey of N = 420 parents of children aged 6-15 attending primary schools in Poznań, Poland. Statistical analyses (Welch's t test, Pearson's χ² test) revealed a digital privacy paradox: despite widespread endorsement of children's right to privacy, as many as 61.6% of parents of children aged 6–15 do not always ask their children for consent before publishing their image, or do not always respect their answers. This practice illustrates the discounting of the child's digital sovereignty from a paternalistic life position. Mothers were more likely than fathers to approach sharenting relationally, seeking digital strokes through the Child ego state. Higher self-assessed knowledge co-occurred with stronger concerns about artificial intelligence and with a propensity for corrective action (41.7% of parents had deleted previously posted photos of their child). The shift toward a position that recognizes the child as a subject occurs in response to adolescents' resistance or to parental self-reflection. The pedagogical implications point to the need for workshops on relational digital maturity and for promoting digital consent from the earliest years.
